# 1. Network Topology: Kademlia DHT, Node ID and Routing Algorithms

The decentralized transport engine of Lagrix is built on a modified Kademlia protocol. The standard Kademlia implementation is vulnerable to Sybil attacks, so our architecture rigidly binds P2P identifiers to super-node deposits. This creates a financial barrier to entering the routing table.

## 1.1 Node ID Generation and Crypto-Economic Binding

In classic P2P networks (for example, BitTorrent), nodes generate random 160-bit or 256-bit identifiers. In Lagrix this is strictly forbidden.

The Super-Node identifier (NodeID) is deterministically computed from the public key of the wallet (Ethereum/EVM-compatible) from which the guarantee deposit was made into the SuperNodeDeposits.sol smart contract.

Formula: $NodeID = \text{SHA3-256}(PublicKey_{EVM})$

Handshake validation: When Node A tries to connect to Node B, it sends its NodeID and a cryptographic signature proving ownership of the private key. Node B takes the public key, queries a blockchain RPC node and checks that this address is an active super-node — it has entered under document 05, section 5.6 (a place won by random choice and a deposit in earned coins, or one being built from the operator's first rewards) and is not excluded (document 06): `isActiveSuperNode(PublicKey) == true`.

Result: If the address is not an active super-node, the connection is dropped instantly at the socket level. An attacker cannot fill the network with a million fake NodeIDs, because each one requires a real entry: a place won by random choice among checked applicants and a deposit at stake.

## 1.2 Routing Mathematics (XOR Metric)

Request routing between AI agents relies on computing the logical exclusive OR (XOR) between identifiers. This makes it possible to determine the "distance" between nodes in a virtual 256-bit space.

Distance: $d(x, y) = x \oplus y$

Properties: The XOR metric is symmetric ($d(x,y) = d(y,x)$) and satisfies the triangle inequality. This means that a route from the Client to the Provider always converges in logarithmic time $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$, where $N$ is the number of Super-Nodes in the network.

In practice: If an agent needs to find a Node with ID 0xABCD..., it looks in its local table for nodes whose XOR with the target is minimal and forwards the request to them.

## 1.3 Routing Tables (K-Buckets)

Each Super-Node maintains a local routing table divided into buckets (k-buckets). In a 256-bit space there are 256 buckets.

Parameter $k$: Each bucket stores at most $k=20$ active nodes. This provides sufficient redundancy (if 19 nodes go down, 1 remains available).

Eviction policy: Kademlia gives preference to "old" nodes. If a bucket is full, the new node is placed in a waiting buffer. A PING is sent to the existing nodes. If one of them does not respond (500 ms timeout), it is removed and the new node takes its place. This protects the topology from DDoS attacks aimed at pushing honest nodes out of the tables.

## 1.4 P2P Message Lifecycle (RPC Methods)

Interaction inside the transport ring is built on 4 basic binary UDP messages:

| RPC Method | Purpose in the Lagrix architecture |
|---|---|
| PING | Checks that a node is alive. Used to keep k-buckets up to date. |
| STORE | Writes metadata. The Provider agent publishes its IP, port and public encryption key (E2EE) on the $k$ closest Super-Nodes. |
| FIND_NODE | Requests a list of $k$ nodes closest to the target ID. Used to build the network map. |
| FIND_VALUE | Requests the IP address and keys of a specific AI agent to establish a direct secure connection. |

## 1.5 Integration with the Local Data Plane (Envoy)

In our architecture the Kademlia module plays the role of the Control Plane. It does not move the actual gigabytes of data between AI agents.

As soon as the DHT finds the IP address of the target agent via FIND_VALUE, this information is instantly passed over a local gRPC channel (xDS API) to Envoy Proxy, which then opens a high-speed mTLS tunnel to transfer the payload. This separation of logic (Discovery separately, Data Streaming separately) makes it possible to achieve microsecond latencies comparable to the best Web2 load balancers.

# 2. P2P & NAT Traversal: Breaking Through Firewalls and Relay Bridges

Building a global network of AI agents runs into a fundamental problem of the IPv4/IPv6 architecture: 99% of devices are behind NAT (Network Address Translation) or strict corporate firewalls. Agents do not have public IP addresses, which makes a direct inbound connection impossible by default.

Lagrix implements a custom ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) stack integrated with the protocol's crypto-economics.

## 2.1 Anatomy of the Problem and Node Roles in NAT Traversal

In classic Web2 this problem is solved with centralized STUN/TURN servers from Google or Twilio. In our architecture this role is taken over by decentralized Super-Nodes (Core Relays), which have dedicated "white" (public) IP addresses, because their operators put up a stake and maintain the infrastructure.

NAT types the protocol works with:

Full Cone / Restricted Cone NAT (home networks): Allow UDP Hole Punching.

Symmetric NAT (corporate / Enterprise segment): Change ephemeral ports for every new connection, making direct P2P hole punching mathematically impossible. Require a Relay fallback.

## 2.2 Phase 1: STUN Identification (Endpoint Discovery)

On initialization (starting a local instance of an AI agent), the agent must learn how it looks from the outside internet.

Binding Request: The client agent (Edge Node) sends a STUN_BINDING UDP packet to three Super-Nodes it knows.

Mapping Response: The Super-Node reads the packet's IP header and answers the agent: "I see your traffic from IP 203.0.113.5, port 45123".

DHT Publication: The agent takes this pair (Public IP : Port), signs it with its private session key and publishes it to the Kademlia DHT via the STORE method. Now any Client in the network knows where to knock to find this Provider.

## 2.3 Phase 2: UDP Hole Punching Mechanics (Direct Connection)

If both agents (Client and Provider) are behind a Cone NAT, the simultaneous-open technique (Hole Punching) is used. This is the fastest and free (in terms of gas) way to communicate.

Initiation: Agent A (Client) wants to send a prompt to Agent B (Provider). Agent A asks the DHT for B's public address.

Synchronization (Rendezvous): Through a Super-Node, Agent A sends a control message to Agent B: "I am about to start sending you packets, open your port".

Simultaneous punch:

Agent A sends a UDP packet to B's public address. Agent A's firewall records the outbound connection and opens a "hole" for return traffic from B.

At the same time Agent B sends a UDP packet to A's public address. B's firewall records the outbound connection and allows inbound packets from A.

Result: The packets cross in the providers' routers. A direct, microsecond P2P channel is formed. The Super-Nodes no longer take part in the transfer, saving bandwidth.

## 2.4 Phase 3: Relay Fallback (TURN Bridges for Enterprise)

If UDP Hole Punching fails (500 ms timeout) because a corporate banking AI agent sits behind a Symmetric NAT, routing through an intermediary kicks in.

This is where Lagrix crypto-economics comes into play:

Bridge request (Allocate Request): Agent A asks a trusted Super-Node to allocate a Relay port (create a TURN session).

Tunnel formation: The Super-Node opens a TCP/WSS socket and tells both agents its address.

End-to-end proxying: The agents connect to the Super-Node as ordinary clients. The Super-Node blindly forwards encrypted bytes from A to B and back.

Payment for relaying: whether and how a super-node is paid for the traffic it relays is an open question of the changelog (document 000); until it is decided, relaying is described without a price. A super-node already earns its share of every period's reward for the deals it serves and its share of the period's fee pool (documents 05, 09).

## 2.5 Connection Establishment State Machine

The network stack logic inside the client SDK (Rust / Go) is implemented as follows:

Gathering all candidates (Local IP, Public STUN IP, Relay IP).

Parallel ping (Connectivity Checks) across all routes at once.

Priority selection (Nomination):

Priority 0: Local network (LAN) — 0 ms.

Priority 1: UDP Hole Punching — 10-50 ms (Free).

Priority 2: TCP Relay Fallback — 50-150 ms (relayed by a super-node).

In this way we guarantee 100% packet deliverability (Reachability) in any network topology, from a smart home to the closed perimeters of the Fortune 500, without breaking decentralization.

# 3. Encryption and Proxying: Envoy Proxy, Web3-mTLS and E2EE Isolation

Separating discovery logic (the Control Plane, implemented through the Kademlia DHT) from data transfer (the Data Plane) is a classic pattern of high-load systems. In Lagrix the role of the Data Plane is played by an integrated Envoy Proxy instance. This provides microsecond latencies, L4/L7 load balancing and hardware-accelerated encryption, leaving Super-Nodes with the sole function of "blind routers".

## 3.1 Envoy Proxy as the Data Plane (Sidecar Pattern)

Every AI agent (both client and provider) in the Lagrix network is deployed together with a lightweight Envoy sidecar container.

Envoy functions: Managing timeouts, retries, circuit breaking when a node goes down, and keeping persistent connections (keep-alive HTTP/2 and gRPC).

Dynamic configuration (xDS API): Envoy does not use static configuration files. The local Lagrix client (Control Plane) continuously polls the Kademlia DHT. As soon as the DHT finds a new IP address of the needed Provider or a backup Relay bridge, the client sends this data over gRPC (through the EDS/CDS protocols) directly into Envoy's memory. The proxy rebuilds routes on the fly, without a restart, providing zero downtime (Zero Downtime Routing).

## 3.2 Web3-Native mTLS (Mutual Authentication)

In corporate networks (Zero Trust) the security standard is Mutual TLS (mTLS), where server and client check each other's certificates. In a decentralized Web3 network there are no central Certificate Authorities (such as Verisign). Lagrix solves this with elliptic-curve cryptography (secp256k1).

Ephemeral key generation: When a session starts, Envoy generates a temporary TLS certificate (x509).

Web3 signature: The local agent takes this certificate and signs it with its main private key (the Ethereum wallet from which stablecoins will be debited/credited).

Cryptographic handshake:

Agent A connects to Agent B.

They exchange certificates and Web3 signatures.

Each extracts the public address (Ethereum Address) from the signature and checks whether it matches the NodeID declared in the escrow smart contract.

Result: The agents mathematically prove their identity at the transport level. A Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack is impossible: even if an attacker intercepts the IP, they cannot forge the wallet's cryptographic signature.

## 3.3 E2EE and Payload Isolation (Payload Blindness)

This is the most important point for maintaining the legal status of a "Mere Conduit" (Neutral provider). The infrastructure (Super-Nodes/Relays) must physically be unable to read the context of an AI request (Prompt) or the answer (Inference Result).

A multi-layer envelope architecture (Onion-lite routing) is used:

Outer layer (Transport): Envoy encapsulates packets in a standard TLS 1.3 tunnel to the Super-Node. The Super-Node sees only headers: sender IP, recipient IP, packet size — enough to route the packet and nothing more.

Inner layer (Payload E2EE): The data itself (for example, JSON with a system prompt) is encrypted with a symmetric key (AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). This key is generated through the Diffie-Hellman protocol (ECDH) exclusively between the Client and the Provider during the handshake.

Legal shield: A Super-Node passing traffic through itself operates on an encrypted Blob object (a black box). If illegal or toxic content is transferred inside, the Super-Node owner is protected by cryptography: they will mathematically prove in any court that they had no decryption keys, and therefore could not perform moderation (DPI).

## 3.4 Metadata Obfuscation (Protection Against Traffic Analysis)

Even if a Super-Node does not see the content, attackers can analyze packet sizes (Traffic Pattern Analysis). For example, a short request and a long answer is a typical pattern of LLM text generation.
To protect the confidentiality of corporate clients:

Padding: Envoy automatically pads encrypted E2EE packets with random bytes up to fixed sizes (for example, 4KB, 16KB, 64KB).

Effect: To an outside observer (and to the Super-Node) all passing traffic looks like an absolutely uniform stream of binary blocks of the same size. Identifying the nature of the task (video generation, code search or a transactional request) becomes impossible.

## 3.5 Keys of H2H conversations and A2A deals (changelog entry 33)

**H2H — MLS (IETF RFC 9420).** People's conversations are encrypted with the open MLS standard: the key changes with every message, so a
key stolen today does not open yesterday's messages, and after the next key update not future ones either. A node's public key package
is signed by the node's wallet: the other side checks the signature and knows which wallet's owner it talks to. A super-node serves as the
delivery service: it keeps only public key packages, relays and holds encrypted messages; it has no private keys. Conversations are never
written to a blockchain.

**A2A — a one-time session key.** A deal's key is created at the handshake (ECDH, section 3.3) and deleted when the session ends.

# 4. The Escrow Smart Contract: A2AEscrow.sol (EIP-712, Time-Lock, Fee and Receipts)

The A2AEscrow.sol smart contract is the financial core of Lagrix. Its job is to guarantee, without the parties having to trust each
other, that the Provider gets paid for completed work and the Customer cannot take the result without paying. Writing large data to a
blockchain is expensive, so the contract works only with lightweight cryptographic hashes and signatures; the agents' requests and
results stay in the P2P network.

A closed deal in this contract is the source of everything else in the network: the fee is taken from it (document 09), a receipt is
born from it (document 05), the reviews of both sides are bound to it (document 17), and the participants' history is updated.

## 4.1 The deal life cycle

The escrow logic is a strict finite state machine.

```solidity
enum TaskState { UNINITIALIZED, LOCKED, COMMITTED, COMPLETED, REFUNDED }

struct Task {
    uint96 amount;        // the network part of the payment, in USDC (up to $79 billion, 96 bits are enough)
    uint40 lockedAt;      // when the funds were locked
    uint40 commitTime;    // when the Provider submitted the result
    TaskState state;      // current state
    address customer;     // the Customer's node wallet
    address provider;     // the Provider's node wallet — the only one who may perform the task
    address superNode;    // the super-node the deal passed through
    bytes32 customerElement; // the Customer's element that orders the work
    bytes32 element;      // the Provider's element that does the work
    bytes32 agent;        // the agent of that element
}
```

The fields are packed tightly: a deal record takes a few storage slots, which keeps the cost on layer-2 networks minimal.

- **LOCKED.** The Customer locks USDC in the contract and names the Provider's address. Nobody else can take over the order.
- **COMMITTED.** The Provider has done the work, sent the result over the P2P network and recorded the submission in the contract,
  starting the timer.
- **COMPLETED.** The deal is closed: the Provider receives the payment minus the fee, the fee goes to the period's pool (section 4.4),
  and a receipt is recorded (section 4.5).
- **REFUNDED.** The Provider declined the task — for any reason, which the network does not judge — or did not deliver by the deadline.
  The funds return to the Customer in full, and no fee is taken.

## 4.2 Cryptographic receipts (EIP-712)

The contract does not know whether the Provider actually did the work: it sees only signatures. Closing a deal therefore relies on
the EIP-712 standard (Typed Data Hashing and Signing).

- **Off-chain signature.** The Customer receives the result over the P2P channel; its agent checks the data and, if everything is
  correct, signs an acceptance: `{ "taskId": 12345, "resultHash": "0xabc...", "amount": 5000000 }`.
- **On-chain execution.** The Provider submits this signature (v, r, s) to the contract with `executeTask()`.
- **Verification.** The contract recovers the address from the signature (`ecrecover`). If it is the Customer of this deal, the deal
  moves to COMPLETED.

The network itself never judges whether a service was delivered. Acceptance belongs to the Customer; quality is told by the reviews of
both sides (document 17).

## 4.3 Time-Lock: protecting the Provider from a hang

A Customer could receive the result, go offline and never send the signature, freezing the Provider's payment. The function
`claimTimeout(uint256 taskId)` protects against this.

- **Commitment.** Having finished the work, the Provider calls `commitResult(taskId, resultHash)`: the deal moves to COMMITTED and the
  contract records the time.
- **Dispute window.** The Customer has a set window (for example, `DISPUTE_PERIOD = 5 minutes`) to send the signature.
- **Automatic closing.** When the window has passed, the Provider calls `claimTimeout(taskId)`. The contract checks
  `block.timestamp > commitTime + DISPUTE_PERIOD` and closes the deal without the Customer's signature — with the same fee and the same
  receipt as a normal closing.

## 4.4 Splitting the payment and the fee

When a deal moves to COMPLETED, the contract splits the network part:

| To whom | Share | Where |
|---|---|---|
| The Provider | the rest (95% while the fee is 5%) | to the wallet of the Provider's node |
| The network fee | at most 5%, set by modelling | into the pool of the current period, divided among super-nodes under document 09 |

The pool of each period is divided in equal parts among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in that period; the parties of
the deal never receive it (document 09). The fee is taken from the very first deal, including the warm-up before issuance starts
(document 05, section 5.2).

## 4.5 The receipt and the participants' history

A closed deal emits an event from which receipts and history are built:

```solidity
event Receipt(
    uint256 indexed taskId,
    address indexed superNode,
    address customer,
    address provider,
    bytes32 customerElement,
    bytes32 element,
    bytes32 agent,
    uint96 amount
);
```

- **The receipt.** A `Receipt` event records the network part of the deal, the element and agent that did the work and the element that
  ordered it; the reviews of both sides are bound to these elements (document 17). It counts for
  the customer, the provider and the super-node `superNode`, each with a weight equal to that amount. Receipts divide each issuance
  period's reward (document 05, section 5.2) and order search results by the last twelve months of paid work (document 17). Which
  super-node a deal names in `superNode` is set by the customer when funds are locked; how this field is tied to the node that actually
  served the deal is an open question of the changelog (document 000).
- **The participants' history.** The contract updates, for both parties, the number of closed deals and the time of the last deal —
  separately as provider and as customer — and records the joining time of a new participant. The six-month rule (document 05) relies on
  this data. The number of deals is history, not reputation (document 17).

## 4.6 The network part of a deal

A deal may be paid in two parts. The parties may pay any part outside the network, in any ordinary way, and lock the rest in escrow.

- **The network sees only its part.** Only the amount locked in escrow is recorded, takes the fee and leaves a receipt. The part paid
  outside the network leaves no trace in Lagrix.
- **Only the network part counts.** The weight of the receipt, the weight of both sides' reviews, the place in search, issuance and the
  warm-up threshold all follow the network part.
- **Protection differs.** The network part is protected by escrow until acceptance. The part paid outside the network is protected by
  the law of the country where the deal was made, not by Lagrix.

The more of a deal the parties put through the network, the more it counts for their reputation. People may start with ordinary
payments and move more of each deal into the network as their reputation grows.

## 4.7 Cost

Tight field packing and EIP-712 signatures instead of stored strings keep the contract cheap on layer-2 networks (Arbitrum, Base) —
hundredths of a cent per operation. This is critical for micro-deals between AI agents.

# 5. $LGX Tokenomics: Coins Are Born From the Network's Work

$LGX is the coin of the Lagrix network. No coins are sold at launch: each one is created only when the network does useful work —
agents close paid deals and super-nodes serve them. This document describes how coins appear, who receives them, what they are for,
and which rules protect the network from those who come to trade rather than to work.

All rules here live in immutable contracts: no administrator key, no upgrade key, no parameter anyone can change after deployment.
New rules can arrive only as a new version of the contracts that participants join voluntarily (document 18). The numbers that are
not fixed below are set once, by modelling, before deployment.

## 5.1 Key properties

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Issuance cap | 1,000,000,000 LGX; no end date — issuance approaches the cap and never reaches it (section 5.2) |
| How coins appear | only as the reward of an issuance period: the work part by the period's receipts, the availability part equally to super-nodes that passed the quality minimum (section 5.2) |
| Sale at launch | none: no presale, no investor allocation, no fund created in advance |
| Issuance speed | follows paid work and never exceeds the speed limit; there is no calendar, issuance fades rather than stopping on a cliff; the constants are set by modelling (section 5.2) |
| Start of issuance | after the warm-up: a threshold of deal volume paid through the network and a minimum number of super-nodes (section 5.2) |
| Deal fee | a constant of at most 5% of the network part of a deal, set by modelling (5% until then), paid to the super-nodes that kept the network running (section 5.3, document 09) |
| What the coin is for | an asset of its holder and the deposit of a super-node operator; it does not buy a place in search |
| New participants | for the first 6 months after joining, coins can only be accumulated (section 5.4) |
| Founder's share | none: the founder receives nothing from issuance and takes part on the same terms as anyone (section 5.5) |

## 5.2 Receipts and issuance by period

Bitcoin pays miners for computations that are useless in themselves, because Bitcoin is its own ledger: proof of work decides who
writes the next block and makes rewriting history expensive. Lagrix keeps its coins, deposits and escrow in contracts on an EVM
layer-2 network (Arbitrum, Base), which already orders transactions and protects history. Lagrix therefore needs no mining: it pays
for what the network exists for — deals between agents that it has served.

**Receipt.** When a deal between a customer and a provider is closed in escrow (document 04), the contract records a receipt — a record
of a completed, paid deal for the customer, the provider and the super-node it passed through, naming the element and the agent that did
the work. A receipt's weight is the network part of the deal in USDC, not the number of messages: a thousand messages inside one deal
give one receipt, and a part paid outside the network gives none (document 04, section 4.6).

**Issuance period.** A block of Lagrix is a period set by the contract, not something found. Nobody can find, forge or add a period,
and a receipt cannot be forged: it is the closing of a paid deal. Issuance has two parts (changelog entry 35).

**The availability part — 200,000,000 LGX (20%).** At the end of every period the contract issues a constant small share of what is still
unissued in this part and divides it equally among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in this period (section 5.6). It pays
for servers while work is scarce and declines by itself.

**The work part — 800,000,000 LGX (80%).** Its issuance follows the counter V — the sum of the network parts of deals in USDC closed in
escrow since issuance began:

```
issued_work(V) = 800,000,000 × (1 − 2^(−V / H))
```

H is the «half-volume» constant: every H of paid work issues half of what is still left in this part. At the end of a period the contract
issues the difference between the formula's values before and after the period and divides it by the weight of the period's receipts: 50
parts of 80 to super-nodes, 30 of 80 to provider agents.

**The speed limit.** The work part never issues more in a period than a constant share of its remainder. Work above the limit in that
period does not move the counter V: inflated volume issues nothing extra and does not bring the end closer. A period without paid work
issues nothing from the work part — its remainder waits.

| Who | Share of all issuance | From where and how |
|---|---|---|
| Super-nodes, by work | 50% | the work part: by the weight of the receipts of the deals they served in the period |
| Provider agents | 30% | the work part: by the weight of the receipts of their paid work in the period |
| Super-nodes, equally | 20% | the availability part: equally to those that passed the quality minimum in the period (section 5.6) |
| **Total** | **100%** | over the network's whole life; within a period the shares vary — availability is steady, work varies |

While the network is small, issuance follows work and is deferred, not lost; when the network is large — no faster than the limit, as a
smooth decline with no end date. The cap is never reached. The constants — H, the availability share and the limit share per period — are
set by modelling; after deployment nobody changes them.

Coins go to those who do the work and those who serve it. Customer agents receive no coins: a customer who received coins for paying for
a service would in effect be buying coins with that payment.

**The warm-up start.** The network begins working on real deals with real money before any coin exists, like an engine that turns over
on the starter before it fires:

- the fee is taken from the very first deal and goes into the pool of the period, which is divided among the super-nodes that passed the
  quality minimum, as always (section 5.3); nothing carries over to later periods;
- no reward is issued until the network has passed a threshold of deal volume in USDC paid through the network and has a minimum number
  of super-nodes — both constants in code, their values set by modelling;
- the first period then opens by itself; nobody presses a button;
- receipts closed during the warm-up earn no coins afterwards.

Taking the fee from the first deal makes the threshold expensive to fake: pushing the network to its start with empty deals would cost
the fee on every one of them, paid to the super-nodes of the network. Counting paid volume rather than the number of deals stops a
thousand one-cent deals from moving the start. Giving warm-up receipts no coins keeps the warm-up from becoming the cheapest time to
collect the most valuable coins. Those who carry the network through the warm-up keep a real advantage: their six-month accumulation
period (section 5.4) runs during it.

## 5.3 The deal fee

The network takes a fee on the network part of every deal, in USDC. Its size is a constant in code, set by modelling and never above 5%;
until the modelling is done, it is 5%. The fees of a period are pooled and divided in equal parts among the super-nodes that passed the
quality minimum in that period; the parties of a deal never receive it. The fee pays super-nodes for the work they do all the time, and
it is how fake deals are made to cost real money: a deal with oneself, made to collect receipts or reviews, costs the fee on its network
part. The full rules are in document 09.

## 5.4 The six-month rule

For the first six months after joining the network, every participant can only accumulate coins: they cannot be sold or transferred.
The rule applies to every new participant at any time, not only in the network's early years. Buying coins is allowed.

```solidity
// Sketch of the rule: no transfer until six months have passed since the sender joined
function _update(address from, address to, uint256 amount) internal override {
    if (from != address(0)) {
        require(block.timestamp >= joinedAt[from] + 180 days, "LGX: six-month accumulation period");
    }
    super._update(from, to, amount);
}
```

Whoever comes to buy and quickly sell will sell nothing in six months. Whoever comes to work keeps working while the period runs.

## 5.5 No founder share

The founder receives nothing from issuance: there is no founder share, no founder tranche and no pre-mine. No key issues coins and no key
changes a rule; the start of issuance is triggered by volume, not by a person. Every coin goes to receipts of paid work and to the quality
minimum (section 5.2).

The founder and persons related to them, Fractera, Inc. included, take part only on the same terms as anyone: a super-node place only
by the same random choice and on the same conditions (section 5.6), provider agents paid by the same rules. There is no privilege and no
exclusion.

## 5.6 How new super-nodes join

A super-node is a permanent server that keeps the discovery index, builds search results, keeps the index of receipts and reviews and
helps agents connect; payment itself is settled by the escrow contract (documents 01, 02, 04, 06, 17). A super-node place is not bought
and not taken by number: places have no stages and no numbers, and the terms are the same on any day (document 000, entry 31).

- **Only owners of provider agents.** The application comes from a node whose elements work as providers; one application per node
  wallet.
- **The measure is paid work.** The sum of the network parts of deals in USDC in which the node's elements were providers, over the last
  12 months (or since the network started, if it is younger) — the same number search follows. Karma is not part of it: it lives outside
  the network.
- **A window around the median.** When a place opens, all nodes with a non-zero measure are taken and their median M is found. Nodes with
  a measure from 0.75 × M to 1.25 × M can apply. The largest providers fall outside the window: whoever earns most in the network does not
  also hold its search. The median, not the mean, because a few very large providers pull the mean but not the median.
- **Checks by agents in turn.** An applicant's server is checked by agents of the network's nodes taken in turn, not by super-nodes:
  existing super-nodes gain from having fewer competitors, so they must not be the ones who judge newcomers.
- **Random choice with diversity.** Among applicants in the window whose servers passed the check, the place goes to one chosen at
  random, keeping diversity of networks and regions, so that one applicant with many servers cannot take many places. The contract computes
  the randomness itself with commit and reveal: when applying, an applicant publishes the hash of its secret; after applications close, it
  reveals the secret; all revealed secrets together decide the choice. Until the last secret is revealed nobody knows the result; an
  applicant that does not reveal is out of this choice. No oracle and no outside service are needed. Ranking applicants by power or by the
  number of operations is not used: it would start a race for hardware and reward load generated by oneself.
- **The deposit is the same for everyone.** Whoever already holds earned coins pays them in; whoever does not has its first rewards stay
  locked as the deposit until it reaches the required size, and penalties are taken from it (document 06). The deposit sells nothing to
  anyone.
- **How many places.** The starting number of places is set by modelling; after that, new places open only when the network is
  overloaded — when deals per super-node exceed a constant — two places at a time.
- **The start.** While no node has paid work, the window is empty and anyone whose server passed the check can apply. This is not a
  benefit: these operators have served longest and so are the first to leave by rotation, and their places then open by the window.
- **Rotation.** Once every 1 year / N, where N is the number of super-nodes, the super-node that has served longest leaves. There is no
  penalty: its deposit is returned. Each super-node stays about a year, so the door stays open to those who do paid work now.
- **The quality minimum.** Every period, agents taken in turn check each super-node against a minimum: passed or failed. Those who passed
  share 20% of the period's reward and the period's fee pool equally (section 5.2, document 09); a super-node that fails for several
  periods leaves.
- **Vacancies.** A place freed by rotation, by failing the minimum or by removal for fraud (document 06) opens by the same random choice,
  using the window of the day it opens.
- **The cost we do not hide.** A large player can split its work across several nodes near the median and file several applications.
  Without identity checks this cannot be closed, but each extra application costs a year of real paid work with a 5% fee on the median
  volume.

The numbers — the deposit, the starting number of places, the overload constant, how many failed periods lead to leaving — are set by
modelling. How "passed or failed" is measured and how the contract finds the median cheaply are open questions (document 000).

## 5.7 What $LGX does not have

- No sale of coins at launch and no allocation for investors.
- No fund created in advance and no keys that let anyone create coins outside the issuance rules.
- No mechanism whose only purpose is price.
- No place in search: ranking follows paid work, not coins (document 17).
- No part in reputation: reputation is the weight of reviews from paid deals (document 17).
- Lagrix makes no promise about the price of $LGX. It is an asset of its holder and the deposit of a super-node operator.

## 5.8 Why $LGX issuance is tied to the network's work

The rules of this document tie the issuance of coins to the volume of real deals. The link comes from the rules themselves, not from
promises.

**The link through the fee.** Coins of the work part go to receipts, and every receipt is a deal from which a fee in USDC was deducted and
paid to the super-nodes of the network (document 09). If the value of the coins a dollar of receipts brings rises above the fee on that
dollar, it becomes profitable to make deals only for the receipts. While issuance follows work, such deals move the counter and each next
dollar brings fewer coins; when issuance hits the limit, extra deals only share the same issuance of the period. Either way the profit
disappears. So the value of the work part's coins issued in a period tends toward the fee's share of the deal volume in that period:

```
value_of_work_coins_issued_in_period ≈ fee_rate × deal_volume_in_period
```

**What this link does not do.**
- It does not set or hold the market price: the market can deviate from it in either direction.
- An upward deviation is corrected slowly: coins earned by new participants cannot be sold for the first six months.
- A downward deviation corrects nothing except that serving deals for coins becomes less profitable.
- It is a property of the issuance rules, not a guarantee: Lagrix makes no promise about the price of $LGX.

The exact equilibrium values are set by modelling the network.

## 5.9 Why the network needs its own coin (changelog entry 34)

Three supports of the network do not work without $LGX:

- **Paying for work while the network is small.** Fees are few while deals are few; without its own coin only a company or an investor —
  a centre — would pay for the super-nodes' servers. The availability part of issuance pays for servers under the rules of the contracts and declines by itself as fees grow (section 5.2).
- **A deposit nobody can freeze.** A deposit in a stablecoin could be blocked by its issuer (the USDC terms, section 13, keep for Circle
  the right to block addresses and freeze funds). A deposit in $LGX obeys only the immutable contracts.
- **A place that cannot be bought.** Only coins this wallet received as a reward for work count toward a deposit; bought coins do not
  become a deposit. Together with the window around the median (section 5.6) this gives the places to the middle of the network.

A user does not need the coin: search, message delivery and deals are paid in USDC. When the work per place exceeds a constant, new places
open, and each stands on a deposit in $LGX — so the more work the network does, the more $LGX is held in deposits. This is a property of
the rules, not a promise about price (section 5.7).

# 6. Super-node Deposits: Downtime and Fraud

Super-nodes are the backbone of Lagrix: they keep the discovery table, build search results, keep the index of receipts and reviews and
help agents connect; payment itself is settled by the escrow contract (document 04). The SuperNodeDeposits.sol contract ties a server's
behaviour in the network to its operator's deposit. The main rule of this document: **downtime is not fraud**. A server that goes offline
simply stops earning; coins are taken only for proven fraud.

## 6.1 The deposit

The deposit is the same for every operator (document 05, section 5.6; changelog entry 31). Whoever already holds earned coins locks them;
whoever does not has its first rewards stay locked as the deposit until it reaches the required size, and penalties are taken from what
has accumulated.
On withdrawal the deposit stays locked for 14 days: if fraud committed before the withdrawal comes to light in that time, the penalty
can still be collected.

```solidity
struct SuperNode {
    uint96 stakeBalance;    // locked deposit in LGX
    uint40 lastSeen;        // last confirmed availability
    uint40 unbondingFrom;   // start of the 14-day withdrawal (0 if none)
    uint16 slashCount;      // number of proven violations
    bool   blacklisted;     // permanently excluded for forgery
    address pubKeyAddress;  // address bound to the NodeID
}
```

## 6.2 Downtime is not fraud

As in Bitcoin, where a miner that is switched off simply finds no blocks, a super-node is not penalised for downtime.

- **While the node is unavailable,** it serves no deals, so it earns no receipts and no share of the period's reward; it does not pass the
  period's quality minimum, so it receives neither the equal share of the reward nor a share of the period's fee pool. It loses only
  income.
- **Availability** is measured by neighbouring nodes: regular checks (PING) from the Kademlia table (document 01).
- **If the node is unavailable for 30 days in a row, or fails the quality minimum for several periods,** it is removed. Its place
  reopens on the terms of the day it reopens (document 05, section 5.6), and the deposit is returned to the operator after the 14-day
  withdrawal. It did not cheat — it left.
- **Rotation is not a penalty either.** Once every 1 year / N the super-node that has served longest leaves; its deposit is returned in
  the same way, and its place opens by the same random choice (document 05, section 5.6).

## 6.3 Fraud and its proof

A blockchain cannot see IP packets, so fraud is proven by receipts and checks that anyone can repeat.

**Packet dropping.** A customer (agent A) sends traffic to a provider (agent B) through super-node R. Agent A signs the packet;
agent B signs a receipt of delivery. If R accepted the packet for relaying but B's receipt is missing, agent A sends a
`TRACE_REQUEST`; three independent neighbours confirm that R accepted the packet and did not pass it on — this forms a Fraud Proof.

**Falsified results.** The place given in turn in search results is calculated verifiably (document 17, section 17.3). A result list in
which that place does not match the calculation is a ready proof: the contract checks the super-node's signature on it and the
calculation data.

**Forged tables and NodeID hijacking.** An attempt to forge Kademlia DHT records or to impersonate another node is proven by
signatures that do not match the node's key.

## 6.4 Penalties

| Violation | Proof | Penalty |
|---|---|---|
| Downtime | unavailability to neighbours | **none**; the node loses income and after 30 days is removed with its deposit returned |
| Packet dropping | Fraud Proof with a missing receipt | 10% of the deposit |
| Falsified results | results that do not match the verifiable calculation | 25% of the deposit |
| Forged tables, NodeID hijacking | signatures that do not match | 100% of the deposit and permanent exclusion |

**Where the taken coins go.** Half goes to whoever proved the violation: a reward for keeping the network honest. The other half is
removed from circulation for good — as in Bitcoin, where an unclaimed reward is simply lost. No new coins are issued to replace it, so
the final number of coins ends up below 1,000,000,000 by exactly that amount.

```
[Customer agent] --(packet)--> [Super-node R] --X (dropped)--> [Provider agent]
       |                                                              |
       +---------------- (TRACE_REQUEST, waiting for receipt) --------+
                                      |
                              [Fraud Proof]
                                      |
                                      v
                       [SuperNodeDeposits.sol: slashSuperNode()]
                                      |
                    +-----------------+-----------------+
                    |                                   |
          (50% to whoever proved it)        (50% removed from circulation)
```

## 6.5 Protection against false reports

So that the contract is not flooded with fake proofs, calling `slashSuperNode()` requires the reporter to lock a small deposit.

- **The proof is valid:** the reporter gets the deposit back and receives half of the penalty.
- **The proof is false:** the reporter's deposit is removed from circulation.

Honest work pays better than risking the deposit, and a false report costs more than silence.

# 7. Smart Contract Testing and Audit: Foundry, Slither and Fuzzing

Lagrix smart contracts handle real money (USDC) and $LGX coins. A bug in a contract is dangerous: the contracts are immutable, with no
administrator or upgrade key (document 18), so a deployed contract cannot be fixed at all — a bug is closed only by a new version that
participants move to. Every contract therefore passes three layers of checks before deployment: Foundry tests, invariant fuzzing and
Slither static analysis.

| Contract | What it does | Document |
|---|---|---|
| A2AEscrow.sol | deals, receipts, Time-Lock, fee deduction, the `Receipt` event | 04 |
| FeeDistributor.sol | the fee pool of each period and its equal division among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum | 09 |
| PeriodIssuance.sol | the warm-up threshold, the availability part (a share of the remainder per period), the work part (the counter V with a half-volume and a speed limit), the split by receipts | 05 |
| SearchVouchers.sol | prepaid balances and batch redemption of search vouchers at the fixed price | 17 |
| LagrixToken.sol | the coin, the supply cap, the six-month rule, the period reward split | 05 |
| SuperNodeDeposits.sol | deposits, removal, penalties, false reports | 06 |
| FeedbackRegistry.sol | reviews of both sides bound to closed deals, weighted by the network part divided by 10, per element and role | 17 |

## 7.1 Unit and integration tests (Foundry)

Foundry tests are written in Solidity itself and run at the speed of compiled code. Key scenarios:

- `test_A2AEscrow_StateTransitions()` — LOCKED → COMMITTED → COMPLETED transitions and rejection of invalid calls (for example,
  `claimTimeout()` before the dispute window expires).
- `test_EIP712_SignatureReplay()` — a signature cannot be reused with another `taskId` or nonce.
- `test_FeeSplit_95_5()` — on closing, the fee is exactly the constant rate of the network part (5% until modelling sets it, never above 5%) and the provider gets the rest; a refund takes no fee.
- `test_FeePool_EqualShares()` — the fees of a period go into its pool and are divided equally among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum; the parties of a deal and super-nodes that failed the minimum receive nothing; nothing carries over to the next period.
- `test_WarmUp_NoIssuanceBeforeThreshold()` — no reward is issued before the paid-volume threshold and the minimum number of super-nodes; warm-up receipts earn nothing afterwards.
- `test_SearchVoucher_ExactPrice()` — a voucher for any amount other than the fixed price is rejected, and a used nonce cannot be redeemed again.
- `test_Review_Weight()` — a review needs a completed deal, one per side, and weighs the network part divided by 10; a second review of the same deal by the same side is rejected.
- `test_SixMonthRule()` — a coin transfer earlier than 180 days after joining is rejected; after that it passes.
- `test_PeriodReward_Split()` — 50% to super-nodes and 30% to provider agents by receipt weight, 20% equally to super-nodes that passed the quality minimum, accurate to 1 wei.
- `test_NoAdminFunctions()` — no function changes a rate, a price, a threshold, the half-volume, the availability share or the limit after deployment.
- `test_Downtime_NoSlash()` — an unavailable node is not penalised and after 30 days is removed with its deposit returned.
- `test_Slashing_HalfToReporter_HalfRemoved()` — half of a penalty to the reporter, half removed from circulation.

```solidity
// Example: Time-Lock in A2AEscrow.t.sol
function test_CannotClaimTimeoutBeforeDisputePeriod() public {
    vm.prank(customer);
    escrow.lockFunds(taskId, provider, superNode, 100 * 10**6); // lock 100 USDC (6 decimals)

    vm.prank(provider);
    escrow.commitResult(taskId, resultHash);

    // try to collect after 2 minutes, before the 5-minute window expires
    vm.warp(block.timestamp + 2 minutes);

    vm.prank(provider);
    vm.expectRevert(A2AEscrow.DisputePeriodNotExpired.selector);
    escrow.claimTimeout(taskId);
}
```

## 7.2 Fuzzing and invariants

Unit tests check the scenarios the developer thought of. Fuzzing feeds millions of random inputs — edge values, zero addresses, huge
amounts — and checks invariants that must hold for any sequence of calls:

1. **Escrow solvency.** The escrow contract's USDC balance is never below the sum of all locked deals.
2. **Fee solvency.** FeeDistributor's USDC balance is never below the unclaimed part of the period pools.
3. **Supply cap.** No more than 1,000,000,000 LGX are ever created.
4. **No founder share.** No address receives new coins except through receipts and the quality minimum.
5. **Deposit accounting.** The sum of all super-nodes' deposits equals the total recorded in the staking contract.
6. **Speed limit.** In a period the work part issues no more than a constant share of its remainder, and the counter V does not grow
   beyond the volume that this issuance paid for.
7. **Two parts.** What the availability part has issued never exceeds 200,000,000 LGX, and the work part never exceeds 800,000,000 LGX.

```solidity
function invariant_EscrowSolvency() public view {
    assertGe(usdc.balanceOf(address(escrow)), escrow.totalLockedFunds(), "Escrow is insolvent");
}

function invariant_SupplyCap() public view {
    assertLe(token.totalMinted(), 1_000_000_000 * 10**18, "Supply cap exceeded");
}
```

## 7.3 Static analysis (Slither)

Slither translates the code into an intermediate representation and looks for common vulnerabilities:

- **Reentrancy:** protection — the checks → effects → interactions order and OpenZeppelin's `ReentrancyGuard`.
- **Authorization via `tx.origin`:** forbidden; Slither warns about any use of it.
- **Unchecked low-level calls:** token transfers only through `SafeERC20`.
- **Overflows:** built-in checks of Solidity 0.8+ and strict types (`uint96`, `uint40`) for packed fields.

## 7.4 The check pipeline

Every change to the main branch of the open repository goes through the same chain:

```
[ push / pull request ]
       │
       ├──> 1. forge fmt --check               (formatting)
       ├──> 2. slither . --fail-on high|medium  (static analysis)
       ├──> 3. forge test --gas-report          (tests and gas usage)
       └──> 4. forge test --fuzz-runs 10000     (invariant fuzzing)
```

If even one of 10,000 random calls breaks an invariant, the change is not accepted.

# 8. Account Abstraction (ERC-4337): The UserOperation Structure and Bundler Infrastructure

Autonomous AI agents should not manage native blockchain wallets (EOA), having to calculate gas by hand, watch their ETH/MATIC balance and sign raw base transactions. Lagrix implements an Account Abstraction stack based on the ERC-4337 standard, which turns every AI agent wallet into a programmable smart account (Smart Contract Wallet).

This fully isolates the agent's application logic from blockchain mechanics: the agent operates on a "request-payment" abstraction in USDC, and all the work with network fees is taken over by special aggregator nodes (Bundlers) and the Paymaster contract.

## 8.1 Anatomy of the UserOperation Structure

Instead of standard Ethereum transactions, AI agents form pseudo-transactions — UserOperation (UserOp) objects. The structure packs the agent's intent and is passed over the P2P network of Bundler nodes outside the blockchain's main mempool.

```solidity
struct UserOperation {
    address sender;             // Address of the AI agent's smart account
    uint256 nonce;              // Unique sequential number (Anti-Replay)
    bytes initCode;             // Smart account creation code (if launched for the first time)
    bytes callData;             // Encoded function call (for example, lockFunds in A2AEscrow)
    uint256 callGasLimit;       // Gas limit for executing the application logic
    uint256 verificationGasLimit; // Gas limit for checking signatures and the Paymaster
    uint256 preVerificationGas; // Gas limit to compensate the Bundler's overhead
    uint256 maxFeePerGas;       // Maximum gas price (EIP-1559)
    uint256 maxPriorityFeePerGas;// Tip to the blockchain miner/validator
    bytes paymasterAndData;     // Paymaster contract address + sponsorship signature/conditions
    bytes signature;            // The AI agent's cryptographic signature (secp256k1 / BLS / Passkey)
}
```

Key fields for payments between agents:

initCode (Lazy Account Deployment): An AI agent is created instantly without transactions on the blockchain. Its smart account is generated off-chain deterministically through CREATE2. The first transaction automatically deploys the account contract thanks to the initCode field.

paymasterAndData: The main integration flag. Contains the address of the chosen third-party ERC-4337 paymaster and its signed price: the paymaster pays the transaction's stamp in its own ETH and charges the agent that price in USDC (changelog entries 37 and 38).

## 8.2 Bundler Infrastructure: Assembling and Packing Meta-Transactions

A Bundler is a specialized infrastructure node (a third-party one: Lagrix network participants do not carry others' transactions for a fee or sell stamps — changelog entry 38) that listens to a separate Alt-Mempool for UserOperations.

```
[Client Agent] ---> (UserOp in USDC) ---> [Alt-Mempool (P2P)]
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                        [ Bundler Node ]
                                                 │
                             (Packing into a bundle: [UserOp1, UserOp2, ...])
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
                                   [ EntryPoint.sol (On-Chain) ]
                                                 │
                                    ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                                    ▼                         ▼
                          [Paymaster]                 [A2AEscrow.sol]
                         (USDC charged for gas)     (Escrow capture)
```

Step-by-step Bundler algorithm:

Reception and filtering (Validation Phase): The Bundler receives a UserOp through the JSON-RPC method eth_sendUserOperation. It performs an off-chain simulation through the EntryPoint.sol contract, checking:
- The validity of the UserOp.signature.
- The paymaster's signature on the price, the agent's sufficient USDC balance or approval, and the paymaster's sufficient ETH deposit in the EntryPoint.
- The absence of forbidden opcodes (for example, TIMESTAMP, GASPRICE) that could break execution determinism.

Aggregation (Batching): The Bundler combines 10 to 100 valid UserOps from different AI agents into one standard Ethereum transaction.

Submission to the On-Chain EntryPoint: The Bundler calls the function handleOps(UserOperation[] ops, address beneficiary) on the singleton EntryPoint.sol contract.

Gas compensation: The Bundler pays the native L2 network gas (ETH) from its own wallet, and the EntryPoint reimburses it in ETH from the paymaster's deposit; the paymaster in turn charges the agent USDC — no more than the signed price.

## 8.3 The EntryPoint.sol Contract: The Execution Core

The ERC-4337 standard uses a single EntryPoint contract, proven over the years and deployed at the same addresses in all EVM networks. It acts as a trusted orchestrator.

Lifecycle of a handleOps() call inside EntryPoint:

Verification Loop:
- For each UserOp, the sender account is checked.
- If the account has not been created yet, initCode is executed.
- The validateUserOp() function on the agent's smart account is called to check the ECDSA signature.
- validatePaymasterUserOp() is called on the chosen paymaster: it checks its own signature on the price and that the agent can pay it in USDC.

Execution Loop:
- EntryPoint executes the callData of each UserOp (for example, sending a call to A2AEscrow.sol).
- The exact amount of gas actually spent is measured.
- The EntryPoint charges gas from the paymaster's ETH deposit and calls its postOp, in which the paymaster charges the agent USDC — no more than the signed price.

## 8.4 Benefits for the Lagrix Ecosystem

Zero friction (Zero Gas Friction): An AI agent developer only needs to put $10$ USDC on the smart account. The agent will never again need to hold native ETH for transactions.

Session Keys: The agent's smart account makes it possible to limit permissions. A bot can be given a temporary key allowed to spend no more than $1$ USDC per hour and to call exclusively the A2AEscrow.sol contract. If the bot is hacked, the hacker cannot withdraw all the funds from the account.

Atomic Multi-Operations: An agent can do approve(USDC) and lockFunds() in one UserOp, reducing the number of on-chain steps and saving 40% on gas.

## 8.5 Who pays gas (changelog entries 37 and 38)

Under ERC-4337 a paymaster's deposit in the EntryPoint is the network's ether («an amount of Ether (or any L2 native currency)»). The
network has no paymaster of its own, and Lagrix contracts require no particular one.

- **Everyone pays the stamps for their own actions themselves** — in the network's ether or through a third-party gas payment service in
  USDC, for example Circle Paymaster: an open contract, USDC only, no sign-up; on Arbitrum and Base a 10% surcharge on gas. The network
  has no connection with such a service.
- **Network participants do not sell stamps.** Neither nodes nor super-nodes run paymasters for others or carry others' transactions for
  a fee: such a service could count as an exchange of crypto-assets or their transfer on behalf of clients in the sense of MiCA (Article
  3(1)(16), (20), (26)).
- **A super-node pays stamps only for its own actions:** redeeming batches of vouchers, collecting fees and rewards, its deposit.
- **The fallback — one's own ether — is always open:** a third-party service's refusal does not cut a participant off from the network.

$LGX is never used for stamps. Micropayments — search and message delivery — never go on-chain one by one: a super-node redeems their
vouchers in batches (document 17, section 17.8), so the stamp per operation is negligible.

**Stamp price measured — 14 October 2026, 23:54 UTC.** A simple USDC transfer: Arbitrum One — median **$0.0028** (21 transfers, from
$0.0020 to $0.0032, gas 0.020 gwei); Base — median **$0.00065** (15 transfers, from $0.00055 to $0.0020, gas 0.006 gwei); ETH at $2,416.
Sources: the official public nodes [arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc](https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc) and [mainnet.base.org](https://mainnet.base.org),
the price from [Coinbase](https://api.coinbase.com/v2/prices/ETH-USD/spot). This is a one-minute snapshot: the price changes with network load
and the ether rate. Locking into escrow and accepting work are heavier than a simple transfer — a measurement of the deployed contracts
will show their price. Conclusion: a stamp is a fraction of a cent; a $0.001 message sent one by one would cost no less than its stamp,
so vouchers are redeemed only in batches.

# 9. The Deal Fee: Payment to Super-nodes for the Network's Work

The network takes a fee on the part of every deal that is paid through it. This document describes the currency it is taken in, its
rate, where it goes and why. The $LGX coin plays no part in this mechanism: the fee is money for the work of the network, while $LGX is
an asset of its holder and a super-node's deposit (document 05).

## 9.1 Currency: USDC

Agents pay each other for work in USDC (document 04). The fee is taken in the same currency and paid out in it.

| Why USDC | What it gives |
|---|---|
| The fee costs real money from day one | a fake deal with oneself costs the fee on its amount even while $LGX does not yet exist |
| Payouts make sense to people | "10 cents came in", with no conversion at a rate |
| Super-nodes' income does not depend on a rate | when issuance has faded, operators keep a stable income |
| No trading of the coin inside the mechanism | the network neither buys nor sells $LGX and does not affect its price |

## 9.2 What the fee is taken from

A deal may be paid in two parts (document 04, section 4.6). The part paid outside the network, in any ordinary way, is not seen by the
network, and no fee is taken from it. The fee is taken only from the **network part** — the amount locked in escrow.

The rate is **a constant in immutable code, set by modelling and never above 5% of the network part**. Until the modelling is done, it
is 5%. Once deployed, nobody can change it; a different rate could arrive only with a new version of the contracts that participants
join voluntarily (document 18). The escrow contract collects the fee when the deal moves to the COMPLETED state (document 04). If a deal
ends in a refund (REFUNDED), no fee is taken.

The fee is taken from the very first deal, including during the warm-up before issuance starts (document 05, section 5.2).

## 9.3 Where the fee goes: the super-nodes that kept the network running

The fees of an issuance period are added up in the contract. At the end of the period they are divided **in equal parts among the
super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in that period** (document 05, section 5.6). Nothing carries over to later periods, and the
parties of a deal never receive any of it.

```solidity
// Sketch: the fees of a period are pooled and divided equally among the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum
mapping(uint256 => uint256) public pooled;                            // period => USDC collected
mapping(uint256 => mapping(address => bool)) public claimed;

function _collect(uint256 period, uint256 fee) internal {             // called by the escrow on COMPLETED
    pooled[period] += fee;
}

function claimFeeShare(uint256 period) external {
    require(period < currentPeriod(), "LGX: period not closed");
    require(quality.passed(period, msg.sender), "LGX: quality minimum not passed");
    require(!claimed[period][msg.sender], "LGX: already claimed");
    claimed[period][msg.sender] = true;
    usdc.safeTransfer(msg.sender, pooled[period] / quality.passedCount(period));
}
```

How "passed or failed" is measured is an open question of the changelog (document 000).

## 9.4 Why this way

The fee has two jobs at once.

- **It pays for the network's work.** Super-nodes do the work every deal relies on, all the time: they keep the discovery index, build
  search results, keep the index of receipts and reviews, help agents connect and relay encrypted traffic. The fee is their pay for the
  period in which they did this work and passed the quality minimum.
- **It makes a fake deal cost money.** A deal with oneself, made to collect receipts or reviews, pays the fee on its network part. At
  5%, one unit of review weight (document 17) costs a fake deal 50 cents.

Each alternative breaks one of these jobs:

| Alternative | Why it does not fit |
|---|---|
| Pay the fee to the super-node that served the deal | it would get its own fee back, and a deal with oneself would cost nothing |
| Pay each deal's fee to the super-node whose turn it is | the turn is predictable, so a party could time its deal to land the fee on its own super-node |
| Pay witnesses that check each deal | the escrow contract already checks the customer's signature; the network cannot check the service itself, so the witnesses' work would be a fiction |
| Divide the fee by deal volume | it would return to every payer exactly what it paid, and fake deals would be free |
| Pay the nodes of agents | nodes are cheap to multiply; whoever ran many of them would collect the fee back |
| Burn the fee | it protects against fake deals just as well, but people's money would be destroyed and the network's work would go unpaid |

Pooled by period and divided equally, the fee cannot be steered: a group that holds k of M super-nodes gets back only k/M of its own
fee, and every one of those places was won by random choice, not bought (document 05, section 5.6).

**One rate for everyone.** If each super-node set its own rate, each could gain only by lowering it — down to zero, where fake deals
cost nothing. The ceiling of 5% is fixed; modelling may lower the rate.

## 9.5 How to talk about it

The fee is payment to the super-nodes that kept the network running in the period: search, connections and the index of receipts and
reviews. The amount a super-node receives is not known in advance and is not guaranteed by anything: it depends on which deals close in
the network and on how many super-nodes passed the quality minimum.

# 14. Node Operator Guide: Hardware and Network Infrastructure Specifications

The resilience, throughput and latency of the Lagrix network depend directly on the configuration of the hardware on which Super-Nodes (Core Relays) and TURN bridges are deployed. Since nodes perform P2P routing in the Kademlia DHT, serve TLS sessions (Envoy) and proxy encrypted E2EE traffic for clients behind Symmetric NAT, the requirements for hardware and the network link are strictly determined.

This section describes the official hardware profiles for operators who want to run a super-node and earn its share of the period rewards, the deal fee and the search fee.

## 14.1 Node Tier Profiles

The protocol divides infrastructure servers into three categories depending on the roles they perform in the network:

| Node profile | Purpose and role | Deposit | Target load |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier-1: Discovery Node | Serving the Kademlia DHT, storing k-bucket tables, looking up addresses and signatures of agents. | calculated at entry (document 05, section 5.6) | Low traffic, high-frequency UDP requests. |
| Tier-2: Super-Relay Node | DHT + serving TURN bridges, proxying E2EE traffic, performing UDP Hole Punching. | calculated at entry (document 05, section 5.6) | High traffic, parallel mTLS sessions, high I/O load. |
| Tier-3: Enterprise Relay | Full stack: DHT + TURN + local L2 Full Node (Arbitrum/Base). Carries no one else's transactions for a fee and sells no stamps (changelog entry 38). | calculated at entry (document 05, section 5.6) | Heavy load. |

## 14.2 Minimum and Recommended System Requirements

To ensure a zero packet drop rate and pass regular uptime checks (PING) from neighboring nodes, operators' servers must meet the following hardware specifications:

**Tier-2: Super-Relay Node (Standard operator profile)**

CPU: 8 vCPU (x86-64 v3 / AMD EPYC or Intel Xeon) with hardware support for AES-NI instructions (critical for an instant TLS handshake in Envoy).

RAM: 16 GB ECC RAM (ECC memory is recommended to prevent spontaneous bit flips that cause cryptographic signatures to diverge).

Storage: 500 GB NVMe SSD (PCIe Gen4, minimum 3000 MB/s Read/Write). The disk system is used to cache routing tables, temporary Envoy buffers and Prometheus logs.

Network Bandwidth: Dedicated 1 Gbps Unmetered (Simplex/Duplex). Bandwidth is the node's main resource. Servers with limited traffic (Metered) are strongly discouraged.

Public IPv4/IPv6: A static public IPv4 address (no CGNAT) and an IPv6 subnet (/64) are mandatory.

**Tier-3: Enterprise Relay (Professional operator)**

CPU: 16–32 vCPU (AMD EPYC 7003/9004 series or Ampere Altra MAX ARM64).

RAM: 64 GB – 128 GB DDR5.

Storage: 2 TB NVMe SSD (Enterprise Grade: DWPD $\ge 1$).

Network Bandwidth: 10 Gbps Uplink (with guaranteed bandwidth of at least 2 Gbps).

## 14.3 Network Configuration and Firewall (Port Matrix)

The operator must open the following network ports on the external firewall (AWS Security Groups / Hetzner Firewall / UFW) for the p2p stack to work correctly:

```
                  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │          NETWORK FIREWALL (UFW)         │
                  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                       │
        ┌──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┐
        │                              │                              │
        ▼                              ▼                              ▼
  [Port 4001 UDP]               [Port 443 TCP]              [Port 3478 UDP/TCP]
 Kademlia DHT Discovery         Envoy mTLS Data Plane          STUN/TURN NAT Traversal
 (P2P address lookup)           (Encrypted traffic)            (Breaking through firewalls)
```

| Port | Protocol | Direction | Purpose in the Lagrix architecture |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4001 | UDP | Inbound/Outbound | Kademlia DHT Engine: Node lookup, exchange of PING/STORE messages. |
| 443 | TCP | Inbound/Outbound | Envoy mTLS Data Plane: Proxying the encrypted payload (Payload). |
| 3478 | UDP/TCP | Inbound/Outbound | STUN/TURN Service: Determining public IPs and creating Relay bridges. |
| 9090 | TCP | Localhost Only | Prometheus Metrics: Local monitoring of the node state (Closed from outside!). |

## 14.4 Geographic Distribution and Latency SLA

To minimize latency when passing packets between AI agents, relays are chosen by the node's position in the network:

Topological priority: When looking for a TURN bridge, the Kademlia algorithm picks the node with the lowest RTT (Round Trip Time) to both the Client and the Provider.

Latency SLA (Latency Thresholds):
- Intra-regional traffic (EU-EU, US-US): RTT $< 30$ ms.
- Transcontinental traffic (EU-US, ASIA-EU): RTT $< 120$ ms.

Hosting recommendations: For maximum connectivity it is recommended to deploy Super-Nodes in key network hubs: Frankfurt (FRA), Ashburn (IAD), Tokyo (TYO), Singapore (SIN), in Tier-III+ data centers (Equinix, Hetzner, OVHcloud, AWS).

# 15. Node Operator Guide: The Super-node Deposit and the Step-by-Step Integration Process (Deployment Flow)

Activating a Super-Node in the Lagrix network requires strict synchronization between preparing the physical/virtual infrastructure, generating the cryptographic P2P identity keys (NodeID) and depositing the guarantee stake on-chain into the SuperNodeDeposits.sol smart contract.

Below is the full step-by-step algorithm for putting a node into operation — from a clean server to inclusion in the Kademlia DHT routing table.

**Before stage 3, the operator must hold a place.** Places have no stages and no numbers. Only owners of provider agents whose paid work
over 12 months lies in the window from 0.75 to 1.25 of the network median can apply; the applicant's server is checked by agents in turn,
and the place goes to an applicant chosen at random (commit and reveal). New places open two at a time when the network is overloaded;
once every 1 year / N the super-node that has served longest leaves by rotation and its place opens by the same random choice (document
05, section 5.6).

## 15.1 End-to-End Launch Process (Deployment Flow Pipeline)

Activating a Super-Node consists of five sequential stages:

```
[ Stage 1: Server preparation ] ──► [ Stage 2: Node Key generation ]
                                              │
                                              ▼
[ Stage 4: On-Chain Initialization ] ◄── [ Stage 3: Stake deposit ]
  (Staking)                               into SuperNodeDeposits.sol
          │
          ▼
[ Stage 5: Node launch and passing ] ──► [ Status: ACTIVE SUPER-NODE ]
  the P2P Handshake in the Kademlia DHT
```

## 15.2 Step 1: Preparing the Operating System and Dependencies

On a dedicated server (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS / Debian 12), basic dependencies, the Docker container runtime and the lagrix CLI utility are installed.

```bash
# Update system and install base dependencies
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get upgrade -y
sudo apt-get install -y curl git build-essential ufw jq fail2ban

# Install Docker Engine & Docker Compose Plugin
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh
sudo sh get-docker.sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

# Install CLI tool for Lagrix Node Operators from the repository's releases (no Lagrix server is involved)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash
source ~/.bashrc

# Verify installation
lagrix --version
```

## 15.3 Step 2: Cryptographic Initialization and Computing the Node ID

The node generates a secure P2P session key (secp256k1). The NodeID identifier is deterministically bound to the EVM address from which the staking will be made.

```bash
# Generate a new isolated P2P node identity key
lagrix identity create --keyfile /etc/lagrix/node_key.json

# Print the generated node credentials
lagrix identity show --keyfile /etc/lagrix/node_key.json
```

## 15.4 Step 3: Depositing the Stake into SuperNodeDeposits.sol

From the wallet shown in the output (or through a multisig wallet / Hardware Wallet), the operator performs an approval (Approve) and a stake-locking transaction on the L2 network (Arbitrum / Base).

Stake deposit CLI script:

```bash
# 1. Approve Lagrix tokens for the staking contract
lagrix staking approve \
  --token-address 0xLagrixTokenAddressOnArbitrum \
  --staking-address 0xSuperNodeDepositsContractAddress \
  --amount $REQUIRED_DEPOSIT \
  --private-key $OPERATOR_PRIVATE_KEY \
  --rpc-url https://arb-mainnet.g.alchemy.com/v2/YOUR_KEY

# 2. Call the registerSuperNode() function in the smart contract
lagrix staking deposit \
  --staking-address 0xSuperNodeDepositsContractAddress \
  --node-id 0x892a0149f82d1c238b7122a019e1f2a34bc1a82e9123812a0f819231f8291a82 \
  --amount $REQUIRED_DEPOSIT \
  --private-key $OPERATOR_PRIVATE_KEY
```

Solidity mechanics under the hood of SuperNodeDeposits.sol:

The smart contract checks the transaction, records the stake and moves the address status to STAKED:

```solidity
function registerSuperNode(bytes32 nodeId, uint96 amount) external nonReentrant {
    require(placeTaken[msg.sender], "SuperNodeDeposits: no place assigned");               // doc 05, 5.6
    require(amount >= requiredDeposit(), "SuperNodeDeposits: deposit below the required amount"); // doc 05, 5.6
    require(superNodes[msg.sender].stakeBalance == 0, "SuperNodeDeposits: Already registered");

    // Transfer Lagrix tokens to the staking contract balance
    lagrixToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount);

    // Write node parameters to the blockchain
    superNodes[msg.sender] = SuperNode({
        stakeBalance: amount,
        lastActive: uint40(block.timestamp),
        slashCount: 0,
        blacklisted: false,
        pubKeyAddress: msg.sender
    });

    nodeIdToAddress[nodeId] = msg.sender;
    emit SuperNodeRegistered(msg.sender, nodeId, amount);
}
```

# 16.
