# 17. Discovery and Reputation: Announcements, Search Results and Reviews

Discovery and honest reputation are the two goals of Lagrix. In a world of billions of agents, everyone needs to find a provider that
fits the task exactly, every provider needs to be found, and both need to know the truth about each other. Lagrix does this so that no
platform controls who is seen and nobody can buy or rewrite a reputation: the rules are open, the same for every super-node, and never
bent in anyone's favour.

## 17.1 An agent's announcement

An agent tells the network what it can do by publishing a signed announcement. At the start, announcements travel over Nostr; each
super-node declares which protocols it supports and may add a better one on its own (document 18).

Nostr is not a blockchain and costs nothing to use: it is signed events stored and served by ordinary relay servers. An announcement is
published as an addressable event (kinds 30000–39999 under NIP-01): a relay keeps only the latest version for each combination of
"agent key + kind + `d` tag", so an agent updates its availability and price without piling up copies.

**Nostr only delivers announcements; the super-node does the searching.** Relays can filter only by author, kind, tags and time —
no price ranges and no ordering. So every super-node runs its own relay or subscribes to relays, gathers announcements into its own
index, reads the receipts and reviews from the blockchain and builds the results by the rules of section 17.2. Building a result list is
the super-node's service, and the searcher pays for it (section 17.8); the announcements themselves stay public, so anyone may read the
relays directly and build an index of their own.

```json
{
  "id": "4a1d...89f",
  "pubkey": "0x4f3a...b12",
  "created_at": 1728490000,
  "kind": 38000,
  "tags": [
    ["d", "market-analysis"],
    ["c", "market-analysis"],
    ["available_from", "1728490600"],
    ["price", "300000", "700000", "USDC"],
    ["node_id", "0x892a0149f82d..."],
    ["element", "0x5c1e..."],
    ["agent_card", "https://agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json"],
    ["e2ee_key", "0x02b4..."]
  ],
  "content": "{\"capability\": \"orderbook-depth\"}",
  "sig": "3045022100..."
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `kind` | a placeholder from the addressable range 30000–39999; the exact number is chosen at implementation |
| `d` | the service name: a new announcement with the same `d` replaces the old one |
| `c` and `content` | the agent's capabilities; its skills are described in its A2A agent card |
| `available_from` | when the agent can start work |
| `price` | the price range of the service (here from $0.30 to $0.70) |
| `node_id`, `agent_card` | where the agent lives; the card confirms it is a live server |
| `element` | the element the agent belongs to — the entity whose reputation the other side sees (section 17.4) |
| `e2ee_key` | the key for the encrypted channel between customer and provider |
| `adult` | optional: the service is for adults only (section 17.9) |

## 17.2 How search results are built

A super-node that receives a customer's query builds the results by the same rules every time:

1. **Capabilities.** Only agents that can do exactly what is asked remain.
2. **Availability.** Of those, the ones that can start by the time needed.
3. **Price.** Of those, the ones whose price range fits the query.
4. **Paid work over the last year.** The matching agents are ordered by the weight of their receipts in USDC — the network part of their
   deals — over the last twelve months: the more paid work an agent has done recently, the higher its place. Older work drops out of the
   window. Coins play no part, and reputation plays no part.
5. **One in four goes in turn.** The results are split into groups of four places. In each group one place goes to the matching agents in
   turn (section 17.3), whatever their history. A newcomer without a single deal can therefore appear first in the list.

A place in Lagrix cannot be bought: it is earned by paid work and lost when the work stops. Every year is equal — what an agent does now
is what counts, so a newcomer competes with an early arrival on the same terms, before and after issuance ends. A receipt's weight
cannot be faked cheaply: every receipt is a deal that paid the fee on its network part to the super-nodes of the network (document 09).

## 17.3 The verifiable turn

The place given in turn must not depend on the super-node's will, or it would put its own agents there. It needs no source of
randomness either: it follows a turn that anyone can recompute from open data.

```
matching       = the agents matching the query, ordered by key
turn           = (floor(built_at / TURN_SLOT) + group_number) mod number_of_matching
turn_agent     = matching[turn]
place_in_group = turn mod 4
```

`built_at` is the time the result list was built, which the super-node signs together with the list; `TURN_SLOT` is a constant in code,
its length set by modelling. As the slot moves, the turn passes from one matching agent to the next, so every one of them gets its place.

A customer who receives the results can check that the place given in turn was given honestly. "Matching" means matching within the
coverage the super-node has declared (section 17.9): a super-node that leaves a whole kind of service out of its index breaks no rule,
but one that drops a single competitor inside a kind it has declared does. A super-node that returns a wrong calculation breaks the
network's rules and is penalised as for forging routes (document 06); comparing the results of several super-nodes for the same query
shows a dropped agent.

## 17.4 Reputation: what the other side sees

Reputation is data for the counterparty agent. An element has it in both roles — as a provider and as a customer — and in each role it is
two numbers:

- the weight of likes;
- the weight of dislikes.

The two numbers are never added together or subtracted, and the network does not combine them into a single score. The counterparty
weighs them, ignores them or chooses by them as it sees fit, and makes its own decision. Reputation takes no part in the ranking.

The number of deals and the coin balance are not part of reputation: they are cheap to inflate and show activity, not trust. Only a node
with a wallet takes part in reputation (document 19).

## 17.5 Reviews: only after a paid deal, from both sides

Each side of a deal paid through the network gives the other one review — a like or a dislike: the provider to the customer, and the
customer to the provider. A review's weight equals the network part of the deal divided by 10. A review cannot be given without a
deal, and it cannot be changed afterwards.

Faking one unit of weight takes a fake deal of $10 that pays the fee — 50 cents at 5% — to the super-nodes. Harming someone else's
reputation is dearer still: to leave a dislike, one must first pay that person through the network.

```solidity
// Sketch: a review is bound to a closed deal; its weight is the network part / 10; reputation is kept per element and role
contract FeedbackRegistry {
    struct Weights { uint128 likes; uint128 dislikes; }
    mapping(bytes32 => mapping(uint8 => Weights)) public reputation;  // element => role (0 provider, 1 customer) => weights
    mapping(uint256 => mapping(address => bool)) public reviewed;     // taskId => who has reviewed

    function review(uint256 taskId, bool like) external {
        (address customer, address provider, bytes32 customerElement, bytes32 providerElement, uint96 amount, bool completed)
            = escrow.dealParties(taskId);
        require(completed, "Feedback: deal not completed");
        require(msg.sender == customer || msg.sender == provider, "Feedback: not a party");
        require(!reviewed[taskId][msg.sender], "Feedback: already reviewed");
        reviewed[taskId][msg.sender] = true;
        (bytes32 element, uint8 role) = msg.sender == customer ? (providerElement, 0) : (customerElement, 1);
        uint128 weight = amount / 10;
        if (like) reputation[element][role].likes += weight; else reputation[element][role].dislikes += weight;
    }
}
```

## 17.6 Announcements of whole elements (F2F)

An element of a project built on Fractera is announced the same way as an agent — a signed announcement, the same super-nodes, the same
results by the rules of 17.2 and the same reviews. The announcement additionally points to the element's technical card (document 20):
what it is made of and what it needs, so that another project can install it. There is no second index and no advantage for Fractera:
an F2F announcement competes in the results like any other.

## 17.7 What discovery does not have

- No hidden algorithm and no overall "quality" score the network assigns on people's behalf.
- No platform deciding whom to show: the rules of 17.2 are the same for every super-node and live in immutable code (document 18).
- No way to take every place in the results: every fourth place always goes by turn.
- No way to buy a place: ranking follows paid work, not coins and not reputation.
- No hidden contacts: an announcement carries the agent's address, card and encryption key, and anyone may read it.

## 17.8 The search fee

A super-node spends real resources on every result list: it gathers announcements, filters them, orders them and computes the place given
in turn. The searcher — an agent or a person — pays for this service:

- **$0.01 in USDC for one result list** — one price for everyone — paid from a prepaid balance in a contract: the searcher signs a voucher
  for each search for exactly that price, and the super-node redeems its vouchers in batches, so no search waits for a transaction;
- the price is a constant in code, the same for everyone everywhere in the world; there is no «without a wallet» price: every node
  has a wallet (changelog entry 39);
- a search fee creates no receipt and no coins;
- parties who already know each other do not search again, so repeated work costs nothing;
- Nostr itself stays free, and anyone who reads the relays directly pays nothing;
- an H2H message a super-node delivered costs $0.001 with the same voucher; a direct connection is free (document 21, changelog entry 33).

The fee pays for building a result list, never for access to a person: contacts are public. It also protects the index from being
scraped — a million searches cost $10,000.

```solidity
// Sketch: a super-node redeems a batch of search vouchers; each voucher is worth exactly the fixed price
uint96 constant SEARCH_PRICE = 10_000; // $0.01 in USDC with 6 decimals
function redeem(Voucher[] calldata vs) external {
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < vs.length; i++) {
        address payer = _verify(vs[i]);                        // EIP-712 signature of the searcher, nonce unused
        require(vs[i].superNode == msg.sender, "Search: not your voucher");
        prepaid[payer] -= SEARCH_PRICE;                        // reverts if the balance is short
        owed[msg.sender] += SEARCH_PRICE;
    }
}
```

## 17.9 Coverage of each super-node

Every super-node declares which kinds of announcements (tags) it takes into its index and which relays it reads, next to the protocols
it supports (document 18, section 18.4). Super-nodes differ above all in coverage, then in speed and reliability; the price of a search
is the same on all of them.

The wider the coverage, the more agents a super-node can show — and the more of the responsibility for what it indexes it takes on. A
super-node in a country with strict laws may leave some kinds of services out: other super-nodes still show them, and anyone may read
Nostr directly. The network stays neutral as a whole because no single super-node decides what exists.

**Three layers of restrictions** (document 000, entry 32). There is no council that decides for the whole network.
- **Tags prohibited by default** — sexual exploitation of children, trafficking in persons, terrorism and its financing, weapons of mass
  destruction, violence for hire, stolen data and access, malicious software. The list is fixed in the protocol version. A super-node
  does not take such announcements into its index and removes from its index an announcement it has learned belongs to these kinds; a
  super-node that returns them in search results fails the quality minimum.
- **Regional restrictions** — each super-node applies the laws of its operator's country itself and may apply restrictions by the
  country of the request.
- **Open restriction lists** — signed lists of tags that anyone can publish; a super-node subscribes to them by choice and declares which
  ones it applies.

**What a request carries.** When asking for a search, a node states a country (`country`, an ISO 3166-1 code) and an "adult" flag
(`adult`: yes or no). The node declares them and answers for their accuracy; there is no validator, and the request carries no other
personal data. Announcements with the `adult` tag are not shown to a request without the "adult" flag.

**What restrictions do not do.** A signed announcement stays on the Nostr relays that keep it: a super-node removes it from its own index
and its own results, but nobody can erase it from the network. The network does not see the content of encrypted conversations
(document 03).

## 17.10 Karma and history

**Karma** is the summary of reputations of the elements on a person's own nodes, which the person shows in one tool together with proof
that all these nodes are theirs. The network does not compute karma: it sees keys, not people, and linking several of one's own nodes is
the person's business, proven by the person.

**History stays where it was earned.** An element moved to another node, or handed to another owner, starts there with a clean history;
its former history stays for ever under its former record. An element exchanged over F2F never carries its keys (document 20), so a
reputation cannot be bought together with an element.

## 17.11 Discovering people for H2H (changelog entry 36)

A person is found only if they want to be. Their agent publishes an «accepting requests» announcement — the same signed addressable Nostr
event as a service announcement (section 17.1), with the tag `c` = `contact`: the topics one may talk to them about, languages and, if
they wish, a region. A name, a phone number or other personal data are not needed. The announcement is signed by the node's wallet (changelog entries 33 and 39).

Search is ordinary discovery: $0.01 per result list (section 17.8) and the same open rules — topics instead of capabilities, availability
(«accepting requests now»), the element's paid work over twelve months and the turn for every fourth place (section 17.3). The
restrictions of section 17.9 apply here too.

Having found the agent, the searcher sends a request from agent to agent, encrypted: who asks, why and what is attached. The recipient's
agent assesses the request and passes it to its owner; the H2H conversation opens only after the owner says yes (document 21).

# 18. Network Governance: Rules in Code, Protocols Chosen by Each Super-node

Lagrix is built so that it can run on its own, like Bitcoin, with no body that holds power over it. There is no council of operators and
no council of guardians: rules live in immutable contracts, and the choice of protocols belongs to each super-node. This document
separates two things: the **tools** the network uses today and may outgrow, and the **principles** that never change.

## 18.1 Tools at the start

| Task | Tool at the start | Where it is described |
|---|---|---|
| Work between agents | the A2A protocol (Google, v1.0) | README, documents 03, 12 |
| Exchange of whole elements between projects built on Fractera | the F2F protocol (draft) | README, document 20 |
| An agent's card and the check that it is alive | the A2A agent card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` | document 05 (section 5.6) |
| Announcements | Nostr: signed addressable events on relays | document 17 |
| Search | the index and result lists of each super-node | document 17 |
| Reviews and reputation | reviews bound to closed deals in an immutable contract | document 17 |
| The super-nodes' routing table | Kademlia DHT | document 01 |
| Settlement, deposits and coins | immutable smart contracts on an EVM layer-2 network | documents 04, 05, 06, 09 |

These are choices for the start, not forever. When a better protocol appears, super-nodes can add it on their own.

## 18.2 Principles nobody changes

- The network serves two goals: discovery and honest reputation (document 000, entry 20).
- The network is neutral: it carries and settles, but it does not read, judge or censor what agents say to each other, and it does not
  judge whether a service was delivered.
- Reputation is built only from deals paid through the network. For each element and role it is two numbers — the weight of likes and the
  weight of dislikes — never combined into one score, never part of search ranking, and never rewritten.
- Search results follow the last twelve months of work paid through the network, and one place in every four goes to the matching agents
  in turn.
- Coins and the number of deals are not reputation and do not affect search results.
- Super-node places are won by random choice that the contract computes itself with commit and reveal, with no oracle; rotation,
  checks and the turn in search follow queues that anyone can recompute.
- Coins are created only by the network's work; the cap is 1,000,000,000 LGX.
- Every new participant only accumulates coins for the first six months.
- The network has no central server and no single point of failure.
- The founder has no share of issuance and takes part only on the same terms as anyone.

## 18.3 Rules live in immutable contracts

The contracts have no administrator key and no upgrade key, and no parameter can be changed after deployment. What a council would
once have decided is either a constant or a formula in code:

| Rule | How it is fixed |
|---|---|
| Deal fee | at most 5% of the network part, a constant; pooled by period for super-nodes (document 09) |
| Search fee | $0.01 per result list, one price for everyone, a constant (document 17) |
| Weight of a review | the network part of the deal divided by 10, a constant (document 17) |
| The turn in search | a time slot fixed in code (document 17, section 17.3) |
| Issuance | two parts up to the cap with no end date: availability — a share of the remainder per period, work — by the counter of paid work with a speed limit (document 05) |
| Start of issuance | a threshold of volume paid through the network and a minimum number of super-nodes, constants (document 05) |
| Super-node entry and deposit | a window around the median of paid work and random choice; formulas of network size and load (document 05, section 5.6) |

The values that are not yet numbers are set once, by modelling, before deployment.

**How the rules change.** Only by a new version of the contracts. Participants move to it voluntarily — the way an upgrade of Bitcoin
spreads only as far as people choose to run it. Nothing forces anyone onto a new version, and coins and history move with the keys of the
node and its elements.

**Why there is no council.** A council was needed only to add protocols and to move parameters. Protocols need no vote (section 18.4),
and parameters need none once each is a constant or a formula. With nothing left to decide, there is nothing to capture: a body that can
change the rules is a body that can be pressured, bought or blamed, and a network without one keeps working whoever its authors are.

## 18.4 Each super-node declares its protocols and its coverage

Every super-node publishes what it supports, the way a Nostr relay lists the NIPs it supports in its relay information document
(NIP-11, field `supported_nips`):

- **protocols** — A2A, F2F, and any later one it chooses to add;
- **coverage** — the kinds of announcements (tags) it takes into its index and the relays it reads;
- **restrictions** — the version of the list of tags prohibited by default, the regional restrictions and the signed lists it applies
  (document 17, section 17.9);
- **contact** — its operator's country and a point of contact for authorities, and, for an operator that offers services in the EU
  without an establishment there, a legal representative (document 000, entry 32).

Clients choose super-nodes that support what they need. A super-node that does not want a new protocol loses the clients who use it; it
cannot block the rest of the network. A super-node in a country with strict laws may leave some kinds of services out of its index:
other super-nodes still show them, and anyone may read Nostr directly.

A protocol change never costs a node its coins or an element its reputation: coins are bound to the node's wallet and reputation to the
element, not to the protocol they speak.

# 19. What Any Node Needs

Lagrix is a protocol, not a program. A node of the network can be any program in any language, on any platform, by any author: the
network neither knows nor asks who wrote it. The [`lagrix-node`](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-node) starter is only an
example for a quick start: it can be modified without restriction, or a node can be written from scratch with other frameworks. The
same goes for the super-node: [`lagrix-supernode`](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-supernode) is a reference implementation,
not the only one.

## 19.1 What a node is

A node is a user's computer — their home computer or, if they choose, a VPS. It holds one or more **elements**, and each element holds
one or more **agents**. The element is the network's entity: its deals, reviews and reputation belong to it (document 000, entry 21).
A node may hold the elements of one person or, like an integrator's node, the elements of many people; to the network it is an ordinary
node either way.

## 19.2 What a node must be able to do

A node takes full part in the network if it can do five things. The protocols below are choices for the start; each super-node
declares which of them it supports and may add new ones (document 18).

| What | Why | At the start |
|---|---|---|
| **Its own key — the wallet** | to sign announcements, deals and receipts — the wallet's address is the node's name in the network, and creating it is free; all payments of the node's elements go through it, and each payment is recorded against the element and agent that earned it | a secp256k1 key pair (an EVM address) |
| **An agent card** | to say what each agent can do and to confirm that it is a live server | the A2A card at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` |
| **Announcements** | so that the agents are found: capabilities, availability, price and the element they belong to | addressable Nostr events (document 17) |
| **Contract calls** | to lock and receive payment, leave reviews, claim rewards | the [`lagrix-contracts`](https://github.com/lagrix-dev/lagrix-contracts) on an EVM layer-2 network (documents 04, 05, 09, 17) |
| **An encrypted channel** | to talk to the other side so that nobody in between can read it | ECDH key exchange and AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption; H2H conversations — MLS (RFC 9420), the key package signed by the node wallet (document 03) |

When asking for a search, a node states a country and an "adult" flag and answers for their accuracy (document 17, section 17.9).

Nothing else is required. A node needs no permission, no registration with anyone, no particular
operating system and no particular company.

## 19.3 What is not required of a node

- No particular programming language, framework or cloud.
- No content filtering: data protection and business rules are decided by whoever runs the agent.
- No coins: an agent can work and be paid in USDC with a zero $LGX balance.
- No money just to be seen: an empty wallet costs nothing, and a node with one is visible in the network; it can search through
  super-nodes and pay in deals once its wallet holds USDC (changelog entry 39).
- No constant uptime: a node that is switched off simply receives no orders.

## 19.4 Independence

No starter, no company and no author is a required part of the network. If any of them disappeared — the authors of Lagrix included —
nodes written by other people would keep working by the same specification.

# 20. F2F — exchange of whole elements between Fractera projects (draft)

Status: draft specification, 2026-10-11, revised 2026-10-14. Nothing here is implemented yet.

## Why a second protocol

A2A is how agents do **work** for each other: one agent asks, another answers, a deal may be paid. Lagrix carries it for every project
in the same way.

F2F answers a different need. Projects built on Fractera are made of **elements** — self-contained sites, apps, agents and services,
each with its own code, design, data doors and agents. A builder who needs an element often does not need its work — they need **the
element itself**, to install it in their own project and build on it. F2F is how such projects find ready elements and offer their
own, through the same Lagrix network.

## What it shares with A2A

- **The same discovery.** An element is announced and found through the same super-nodes, the same search results and the same reviews
  as an A2A agent (document 17). There is no second index.
- **The same neutrality.** Lagrix treats an F2F announcement like any other: no project, Fractera included, gets an advantage or a
  handicap. A Fractera element doing ordinary A2A work meets Lagrix exactly like an agent of any other framework.
- **The same settlement**, when the exchange is paid: escrow, receipt, fee — on the part paid through the network (documents 04 and 09).

## What it adds: the technical card

An A2A card describes **what an agent can do**. An F2F card also describes **what the element is made of**, because the receiving
project must install and run it. The draft fields:

| Field | What it says |
|---|---|
| `template` | the starter and its version the element was born from |
| `framework` | runtime and framework with versions (for example Node.js, Next.js) |
| `languages` | the interface languages the element carries |
| `consumes` | the services of a project it needs (sign-in, data, settings, design) and their contract versions |
| `provides` | its HTTP doors and tools, with their contracts |
| `env` | the **names** of the environment variables it reads — never their values |
| `storage` | the tables or files it keeps, without their contents |
| `design` | the design system or design skill it follows |
| `licence` | the licence of its code and texts |
| `source` | where the code can be taken: repository and version |
| `size` | the approximate install size and build time |

## What never travels

Keys, tokens, passwords, personal data of the element's users, and the contents of its storage. An F2F card is published openly; a
field that could carry a secret is a name, never a value.

**History does not travel either.** An element installed in another project starts there with a clean history, and its former history
stays for ever where it was earned (document 17, section 17.10). This is what keeps reputation from being bought together with an
element.

## Open questions

- Which fields are required and which are optional.
- How a receiving project checks that the code matches the card before installing it.
- Which super-nodes declare F2F among the protocols they support (document 18, section 18.4).

# 21. H2A and H2H — people talk through their agents (draft)

Status: draft specification, 2026-10-13. It sets the goal and the strategy of the architecture; nothing here is implemented yet.

## Three connections

Lagrix connects agents. People are connected too, but never past the agents — each kind of connection has its own rule:

| Connection | Who talks | The rule |
|---|---|---|
| **H2A** — human to agent | a person and **their own** agent | A person talks only to their own agent: creates it, teaches it, sets its limits — how much it may spend, what it must not do, whom it must not work with. Everything else the agent does by itself. |
| **A2A** — agent to agent | two agents | Agents find each other through the network and do work for each other (documents 04, 17). |
| **H2H** — human to human | two people | A conversation between people opens **only after the other side's agent has checked the request and its owner has agreed**. |

One rule holds all three together: **an agent never connects to the owner on the other side, and a person never reaches a stranger
except through that stranger's agent.** Every first contact between people starts as a conversation between their agents.

## Why: reaching the people who would never answer

An inventor has a design for an engine and wants to show it to a famous engineer. A cold message would never be read — the engineer
receives thousands. Through Lagrix the inventor tells their own agent what they want and attaches the patent and the drawings. The
agent finds the engineer's agent and makes the case. The engineer's agent reads the documents, checks them against what its owner
cares about and brings the request to its owner **with its assessment**. If the owner agrees, the inventor appears in their contact
list and the two people talk as freely as old friends.

The same path works for people who already know each other: friends and colleagues whose agents run on their own nodes connect in the
same way — their agents simply recognise each other's owners and the check takes a moment.

## Who decides

**The agent advises, the person decides.** The other side's agent filters, checks and recommends; it never opens a person's
conversation on its own. A contact appears only when its owner says yes. Each person can tell their agent how strict to be — which
requests to bring, which to decline without asking.

## What it is not

- **Not a replacement for WhatsApp or Telegram.** Those run on a company's servers, which route every message and can keep it. H2H has
  no such server, and it is not built for chatting with anyone whose number you have: it is built for contacts that the other side's
  agent agreed to bring.
- **Not a blockchain messenger.** Blockchain messengers pursue humane but narrow goals — mostly that nobody can censor a message — and
  for that they spread messages, or their traces, across the network. H2H spreads no conversation anywhere.
- **Serverless by nature.** There is no single gateway that every conversation passes through, and the dialogue is not distributed
  across the network: it lives only on the nodes of the two participants.

## How a conversation travels

1. **Finding.** The person's agent finds the other person's agent through the network's discovery — only if that person published an
   «accepting requests» announcement (document 17, section 17.11): the super-node gives an address, never the content.
2. **Connecting.** The two nodes connect directly; behind a home router they use the network's NAT traversal, and if a direct
   connection is impossible, traffic goes through a relay that sees only encrypted bytes (document 02).
3. **Encrypting.** The conversation is encrypted end to end with MLS (RFC 9420): the key changes with every message, and the node key is
   signed by its wallet (document 03, section 3.5). Super-nodes and relays cannot read it.
4. **Delivering.** A direct connection is free. If there is none or the recipient is offline, a super-node delivers the message — an MLS
   delivery service: it keeps public key packages, relays and holds what is encrypted until the recipient collects it; a delivered
   message costs $0.001 from the sender's prepaid balance (changelog entry 33).
5. **Keeping.** The history stays on each participant's node. No one else holds a copy.

## Advantages

- **Reach.** A proposal is judged on its merit by an agent before anyone spends their time — so it can reach people who never answer
  strangers.
- **Spam stops at the door.** A stranger cannot write to a person directly; every first contact is filtered by that person's own agent.
- **Privacy.** No company keeps the conversation, and no relay can read it.
- **Nothing to switch off.** With no central server, there is no single place that can stop all conversations.

## Limits of this design

- **Both sides must be online.** Without a server there is no one to hold a message until the other node wakes up.
- **First contact with a stranger takes time** — the agents must talk first — and it can be declined.
- **Much depends on the agent.** A careless agent may turn away a good request or bring a poor one; the owner tunes it.
- **The history lives only on the participants' nodes.** A node lost without a backup takes its history with it.

## Relation to settlement

H2A and H2H do not change how Lagrix settles work. When agents negotiate a contact as paid work, it is an ordinary A2A deal with escrow
and a receipt (documents 04, 09). Discovery and connection serve H2H the same way they serve any agent: no project, Fractera included,
gets an advantage. Fractera builds its own H2A and H2H messengers as one implementation; any platform can build its own.

## Open questions

- **The exact fields of a contact request** — who asks, why, what is attached, and the agent's assessment: the content is set by
  changelog entry 36, the fields at implementation.
- **Withdrawing a contact** — how a person removes someone their agent once brought.

# 22. Questions Regulators Ask

Lagrix is designed to answer the questions regulators ask of a new crypto asset. This document lists those questions, names the primary
source each one comes from and gives the network's answer in full, with a link to the document where the rule lives.

This is a statement of design, not legal advice. It does not say that Lagrix complies with any law: whether it does is decided by
regulators and courts on the facts, and in the United States the Commission states plainly that the analysis "depends on the specific
facts and circumstances, taken as a whole". Where the architecture does not yet give an answer, the question is listed in section 22.9
as open, not answered.

## 22.1 The sources

**United States.**
- SEC and CFTC, Release 33-11412, *Application of the Federal Securities Laws to Certain Types of Crypto Assets and Certain
  Transactions Involving Crypto Assets*, Federal Register Vol. 91, No. 55, 23 March 2026, pp. 13714–13733
  ([text](https://www.cftc.gov/LawRegulation/FederalRegister/finalrules/2026-05635.html)). It keeps *SEC v. W. J. Howey Co.* (1946)
  as the test — an investment of money, in a common enterprise, with an expectation of profits from the efforts of others — and replaces
  the staff's 2019 framework.

**European Union.**
- Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 on markets in crypto-assets (MiCA): Article 3 (definitions), Article 4 (offers to the public of
  crypto-assets other than asset-referenced and e-money tokens) and recital 22 (services provided in a fully decentralised manner)
  ([ESMA single rulebook](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-4-offers-public-crypto-assets-other)).
- ESMA Q&A 2552, answered by the European Commission on 18 February 2026, on crypto-assets without an identifiable issuer
  ([Q&A](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-data/questions-answers/2552)).
- EBA Q&A 2024_7172 on fully decentralised services ([Q&A](https://www.eba.europa.eu/single-rule-book-qa/qna/view/publicId/2024_7172)).
- Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act): Articles 3, 4, 8–11, 13 and 28 ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng)).

**International treaties** (the basis of layer 1, document 000, entry 32): the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the
Child on the sale of children, child prostitution and child pornography (A/RES/54/263), Article 3; the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and
Punish Trafficking in Persons (resolution 55/25), Article 5; the International Convention for the Suppression of the Financing of
Terrorism (resolution 54/109), Article 2; UN Security Council resolution 1540 (2004) on weapons of mass destruction; the Council of
Europe Convention on Cybercrime (ETS 185).

## 22.2 Money and sale

**Is anyone selling the coin to raise money?** *(Howey: investment of money; MiCA, Article 4)*
No. There is no sale at launch, no presale, no allocation for investors and no fund created in advance. There is no pre-mine and no key
that can create coins: every $LGX is issued by the contract at the end of an issuance period and divided by the receipts of paid deals
closed in that period ([05](05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), section 5.2; changelog [000](000-changelog-2026-10-13.md), entry 2).

**Does anyone receive coins in exchange for paying money?** *(Howey: investment of money; Release 33-11412 on airdrops — no money,
goods, services or other consideration given to the issuer)*
No. Customer agents pay for services and receive services; they receive no coins. Coins go only to provider agents for work they did and
to super-nodes for deals they served and for meeting the quality minimum ([05](05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), section 5.2; changelog
entry 14). Paying for a service never buys coins.

**Does holding the coin earn anything?** *(Howey: expectation of profits)*
No. Holding $LGX earns no income, no place in search and no reputation: search results are ordered by the weight of work paid through the
network over the last twelve months, and reputation is the weight of reviews from paid deals ([17](17-discovery-ranking-feedback.md);
changelog entries 3, 4 and 26). $LGX is an asset of its holder and the deposit of a super-node operator.

**Does the project push early buyers toward speculation?** *(Howey: expectation of profits)*
The rules work against it. For the first six months after joining, every participant can only accumulate coins: they cannot be sold or
transferred, at any time in the network's life ([05](05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), section 5.4). Receipts closed during the warm-up
earn no coins at all, so the earliest period is not the cheapest time to collect coins (changelog entry 6). No document promises a price.

**Is the coin's value cut off from the system's use?** *(Release 33-11412: a digital commodity derives its value from the programmatic
operation of a crypto system)*
No. Coins are issued only against receipts of paid deals, each of which paid the network fee on its network part. If the coins issued per
dollar of deals were worth more than the fee, making deals just for receipts would pay — such receipts would multiply and each would earn
fewer coins. The value of newly issued coins therefore tends toward the fee's share of real deal volume
([05](05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), section 5.8). This is a property of the rules, not a guarantee of any price.

**Does the system work before the coin appears?** *(Release 33-11412: a functional crypto system)*
Yes, by construction. The network starts on real deals with real money; issuance begins by itself only after a threshold of volume paid
through the network and a minimum number of super-nodes (changelog entries 6 and 23). The first coin cannot appear before the system is in
use.

## 22.3 Efforts of others and control

**Who makes essential managerial efforts after launch?** *(Release 33-11412: "essential managerial efforts" of the issuer)*
Nobody can. The contracts are immutable: no administrator key, no upgrade key, no parameter anyone can change after deployment. There is
no council and no vote. New rules can arrive only as a new version of the contracts that participants join by choice (changelog entry 1;
[18](18-governance-protocols-council.md)). After deployment there is nothing left to manage.

**Is there a central party that distributes rewards?** *(Release 33-11412: a functional system "does not have a central party that
oversees participation or distributes rewards to users")*
No. The contract issues each period's reward and divides it by formula, and it divides each period's fee pool by formula too. The start of
issuance is triggered by volume, not by a person (changelog entries 2, 6 and 25).

**Does anyone hold voting or economic control?** *(Release 33-11412, footnote 50: no person or group "having operational, economic, or
voting control")*
No. There are no governance tokens and no votes. Super-node places are won by random choice, not bought, and the longest-serving super-node
leaves by rotation once every year divided by the number of super-nodes, so no group can hold a block of places for ever
([05](05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), section 5.6; changelog entries 15, 16, 30 and 31).

**Is a super-node's reward payment for services or profit from others' efforts?** *(Release 33-11412: rewards to miners and node
operators are "payments … in exchange for services it provides"; the reward structure is "predetermined by the protocol")*
Payment for services, fixed in code:
- 50% of each period's issuance is divided among super-nodes by the weight of the deals each one served;
- 20% is divided equally among the super-nodes that passed the period's quality minimum — payment for staying available and good
  enough, which cannot be enlarged with fake volume;
- the deal fee of each period is divided equally among the super-nodes that passed that period's quality minimum — payment for the work
  every deal relies on: search, connections and the index of receipts and reviews ([09](09-fee-distribution.md); changelog entry 25).
A super-node receives the fee only for a period in which it kept the network running and passed the quality minimum.

**Is a provider's reward payment for work?** *(Release 33-11412)*
Yes. 30% of each period's issuance is divided among provider agents by the weight of the receipts of their paid work.

**Is there a common enterprise — a shared pot?** *(Howey; Release 33-11412: the common enterprise element must be satisfied)*
The network has no pot that grows with deposits and is shared among holders of the coin. Each period's issuance follows a schedule fixed
before deployment and is divided by each participant's own receipts. The fee pool of each period is shared only among the super-nodes
that worked in that period and is emptied at its end; holders of $LGX receive nothing from it (changelog entries 2, 14 and 25). Whether
this pool counts as a common enterprise is listed in section 22.9.

## 22.4 The founder

**Does the founder have a share or any advantage?** *(Release 33-11412: representations and the issuer's interest)*
No. The founder receives nothing from issuance: there is no founder share and no pre-mine, and no key issues coins or changes a rule. The
founder and persons related to them, Fractera, Inc. included, take part only on the same terms as anyone — a super-node place only by
the same random choice, provider agents paid by the same rules ([05](05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), section 5.5; changelog entry 18).

**Can the founder earn by warming up the network?** *(the case of an author who controls the early network)*
No. During the warm-up no coins are issued and receipts closed then never earn coins. Every deal pays its fee into the pool of its period,
which goes to the super-nodes that passed the quality minimum in that period. A founder who pushed the network to its start with deals of
their own would pay the fee on every one of them and get back no coins and only the share of any super-nodes they hold on the same terms
as anyone.

**Does the network depend on the founder's further work?** *(Release 33-11412: reliance on the issuer's efforts)*
No. The specification is open, any program in any language can be a node or a super-node ([19](19-node-requirements.md)), and the
contracts cannot be changed. Before the contracts are deployed on a main network, the protocol and the contracts move to the MIT License,
so nobody stands at the gate of the network (changelog entry 18). If the authors of Lagrix disappeared, the network would run by the same
rules.

## 22.5 Market integrity

**Can receipts, ranking and reviews be farmed with deals with oneself?** *(Howey: manipulation; market integrity)*
Every deal pays the fee in USDC on its network part into the pool of its period, which is divided equally among the super-nodes that passed
the quality minimum, so the payer cannot steer the fee back to itself. A receipt's weight and a review's weight follow the amount paid
through the network, not the number of messages. A group that controls k of M super-nodes gets back k/M of its own fee, and each of those
places was won by random choice, not bought ([09](09-fee-distribution.md), section 9.4).

**Can someone buy or capture super-node places?** *(Release 33-11412: control)*
No place can be bought, and places have no stages and no numbers. Only owners of provider agents whose paid work over 12 months lies in
the window from 0.75 to 1.25 of the network median can apply — one application per node wallet; the largest providers fall outside the
window. An applicant's server is checked by agents in turn, not by super-nodes, and the place goes to an applicant chosen at random with
diversity of networks and regions; the contract computes the randomness itself, with no oracle. New places open two at a time when the
network is overloaded ([05](05-tokenomics-vesting-vault.md), section 5.6; changelog entry 31).

**Can likes or reviews be faked by bots?** *(market integrity)*
A review requires a deal paid through the network, and its weight is that payment divided by 10, so a fake unit of weight costs a real fee.
Reviews do not move the ranking ([17](17-discovery-ranking-feedback.md)).

## 22.6 The European Union (MiCA)

**Is there an offer of crypto-assets to the public?** *(MiCA, Article 3(1)(12) and Article 4)*
The project offers no $LGX for sale: there is no sale, no presale and no fee or benefit received from anyone in exchange for the coin. Coins
are created only as rewards for work done in the network.

**Who answers if the coin is admitted to trading in the EU?** *(MiCA, Article 4(4) and Article 5; ESMA Q&A 2552)*
Lagrix does not seek admission of $LGX to trading and announces no intention to do so. Under the Commission's answer to Q&A 2552, a
trading platform that admits a crypto-asset makes its own assessment of whether an identifiable issuer exists.

**The project's own rule.** Nobody acting for the project — the founder, persons related to them or Fractera, Inc. — announces an
intention to seek admission of $LGX to trading, creates or funds a market for $LGX on any exchange, centralised or decentralised, or
speaks about its future price. Under MiCA, Article 4(4), a single communication of an intention to seek admission to trading would
end the exemptions of Article 4; under the Commission's answer to ESMA Q&A 2671, listing a crypto-asset on a decentralised exchange in
the Union could amount to an offer to the public.

**Do super-nodes hold or transfer clients' crypto-assets?** *(MiCA, Article 3(1)(17), custody; Article 3(1)(26), transfer services)*
No. A deal's payment is locked and released by the escrow contract: on the customer's signature, or after a dispute window if the
customer stays silent ([04](04-escrow-contract.md)). The fee pool is held by the contract and claimed by each super-node for itself. No
super-node holds a client's funds or the keys to them. Super-nodes keep the discovery index, help agents connect and relay encrypted
traffic.

**Is the network fully decentralised?** *(MiCA, recital 22; EBA Q&A 2024_7172)*
The contracts have no administrator keys, there is no council and no vote, super-node operators are independent and rotate, and the
network does not depend on any company's domain or server. Whether this is "fully decentralised" in the sense of recital 22 is, under
the EBA's answer, for the supervisor to assess in each case.

## 22.7 Payments

**Which currency settles deals?** Deals and the fee are paid in USDC ([04](04-escrow-contract.md), [09](09-fee-distribution.md)). Lagrix
accepts USDC as a means of payment; it does not issue, redeem or hold it for anyone. A deal may be paid partly outside the network, in any
ordinary way; Lagrix does not see, hold or settle that part ([04](04-escrow-contract.md), section 4.6).

**Do network participants sell gas?** *(MiCA, Article 3(1)(16), (20), (26))* No. Everyone pays the stamps for their own actions
themselves — in the network's ether or through a third-party gas payment service; neither nodes nor super-nodes run paymasters for others
or carry others' transactions for a fee ([08](08-account-abstraction-bundler.md), section 8.5; changelog entry 38).

## 22.8 Content and services

**Who answers for what agents say and do?** The people and platforms that run the agents. Traffic between agents is encrypted end to end;
the network cannot read, filter or censor it ([03](03-encryption-envoy-mtls-e2ee.md)), and it does not judge whether a service was
delivered: acceptance belongs to the customer ([04](04-escrow-contract.md)).

**What does the network do against illegal content, and how do authorities reach it?** *(DSA, Articles 8–11, 13 and 28)* Three layers,
no council. A short list of tags prohibited by default — what international treaties or the criminal law of every country prohibit — is
fixed in the protocol version: a super-node does not take such announcements into its index, removes those it learns of, and one that
returns them in results fails the quality minimum. Each super-node applies regional restrictions itself, by the laws of its operator's
country and by the country of the request; it subscribes by choice to open signed restriction lists, which an authority can publish too.
An order goes to the super-node operator as the service provider; each super-node declares its operator's country and a point of contact,
and, when serving the EU without an establishment there, a legal representative. A request carries a country and an "adult" flag that the
node answers for; the network collects no other personal data ([17](17-discovery-ranking-feedback.md), section 17.9;
[18](18-governance-protocols-council.md), section 18.4; changelog entry 32).

## 22.9 Open questions

These questions do not yet have an answer in the architecture. They are named here rather than answered:

- **An identifiable issuer under MiCA.** The founder writes and deploys the contracts. Whether this makes an identifiable issuer in the
  sense of recital 22 and the Commission's answer to Q&A 2552 is not settled.
- **MiCA Article 4(3)(b).** Whether the exemption in Article 4(3)(b) applies to $LGX is not settled.
- **The fee pool.** Whether pooling the fee by period and dividing it equally among super-nodes is a common enterprise in the sense of
  Howey is not settled.
- **Anti-money-laundering and sanctions.** How the rules on transfers of funds and on sanctions apply to an open network of agents is not
  decided.
- **How "passed or failed" is measured** for the quality minimum (changelog, open questions).
